Part 3: Providers & Resources — Bridging HCL to Real Cloud Infrastructure

Providers are the magic that makes Terraform multi-cloud — each one is a Go plugin translating HCL into cloud API calls. Resources are the building blocks — every VPC, EC2 instance, RDS database, and S3 bucket you'll ever create. In Part 3, you'll provision the complete anihpj/jobpost infrastructure on AWS with Docker and Kubernetes, master resource lifecycle rules, and learn the critical distinction between in-place updates and destroy/recreate — a heavily tested exam topic (~20% of your score).

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~6 hours 📖 Ch 6-8 ☁️ AWS + K8s 🎯 Domain 3

Chapter 6: Providers — The Bridge to Infrastructure 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 6: Providers — The Universal Adapters That Connect Terraform to Everything

Providers are the magic that makes Terraform multi-cloud. Each provider is a Go plugin that translates HCL resource declarations into the specific API calls of a platform — AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Datadog, GitHub, and 3000+ more. Understanding providers deeply is essential because every resource you create depends on them.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🔌 Providers 🌐 Multi-Cloud

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ How providers work internally — the adapter pattern that translates HCL to API calls
  • ✅ Provider configuration — authentication, regions, aliases for multi-region
  • ✅ Version constraints — how ~> 5.0 protects you from breaking changes
  • ✅ The major providers — AWS (4B+ downloads), Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Docker
  • ✅ Multiple provider configurations for multi-region and multi-account setups
  • ✅ How terraform init downloads and caches provider binaries

6.1 Provider Architecture — How Terraform Talks to Clouds

A provider is a Go binary (~100-500MB) that acts as a translator between Terraform Core and a cloud platform's REST API. Terraform Core speaks a generic resource language. The provider translates that into specific API calls.

🧠 Exam Focus: Provider Version Constraints

The exam tests provider versioning extensively. Key points to remember:

  • version = "~> 5.0" — allows 5.x but NOT 6.0 (rightmost component only)
  • version = ">= 4.0, < 5.0" — explicit range (pessimistic constraint is clearer)
  • Provider versions are pinned in .terraform.lock.hcl — COMMIT this file to Git
  • terraform init -upgrade — upgrades providers to latest within constraints
  • Providers are downloaded from the Terraform Registry at registry.terraform.io
PROVIDER ARCHITECTURE — The Adapter Pattern
  TERRAFORM PROVIDER = Translator between HCL and Cloud APIs

  ┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────┐
  │  main.tf    │────────▶│  AWS PROVIDER    │────────▶│ AWS API  │
  │  (HCL)      │         │  (Go Binary)     │         │ (REST)   │
  │             │         │                  │         │          │
  │ resource    │         │ Translates HCL   │         │ Creates  │
  │ "aws_vpc"   │         │ → AWS API calls  │         │ VPC in   │
  │ "main" {    │         │                  │         │ your     │
  │   cidr =    │         │ Handles:          │         │ account  │
  │   "10.0..." │         │ • Auth (IAM/STS) │         │          │
  │ }           │         │ • Retries         │         │          │
  └─────────────┘         │ • Error handling  │         └──────────┘
                          │ • State mapping   │
  Same HCL,               └──────────────────┘
  different provider:
  ┌─────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────┐
  │  main.tf    │────────▶│  AZURE PROVIDER  │────────▶│ Azure    │
  │  (HCL)      │         │  (Go Binary)     │         │ REST API │
  │             │         │                  │         │          │
  │ resource    │         │ SAME HCL pattern  │         │ Creates  │
  │ "azurerm_   │         │ → Different API  │         │ VNet in  │
  │ virtual_    │         │ → Same workflow!  │         │ Azure    │
  │ network"... │         │                  │         │          │
  └─────────────┘         └──────────────────┘         └──────────┘

  💡 KEY INSIGHT: You learn HCL ONCE, deploy to ANY cloud.

Deep Dive: What Happens During terraform init?

The provider initialization lifecycle is one of the most important processes to understand. Here's exactly what happens when you run terraform init:

PROVIDER INITIALIZATION LIFECYCLE — terraform init Step-by-Step
1
Parse required_providers
Terraform reads terraform { required_providers { ... } } blocks from ALL .tf files in the directory
→
2
Resolve Source Address
source = "hashicorp/aws" → expands to registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws using the default hostname
→
3
Check Version Constraint
Reads version = "~> 5.0", queries registry API for available versions, finds the newest matching version (e.g., 5.82.0)
→
4
Check Lock File
If .terraform.lock.hcl exists, verifies checksums match. If hashes differ → error (provider binary changed!)
→
5
Download Binary
Fetches provider binary from releases.hashicorp.com (official) or GitHub Releases (community). Saved to .terraform/providers/
→
6
Verify Signature
HashiCorp-signed providers are verified against HashiCorp's GPG key. Community providers have SHA256 checksum verification.
→
7
Update Lock File
Writes/updates .terraform.lock.hcl with exact version + platform-specific checksums (windows_amd64, linux_amd64, darwin_arm64)

Understanding .terraform.lock.hcl — The Dependency Lock File

.terraform.lock.hcl — Anatomy of a Lock File
provider "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws" {
  version     = "5.82.0"
  constraints = "~> 5.0"
  hashes = [
    "h1:ABCD1234...",  # linux_amd64 SHA256
    "h1:EFGH5678...",  # darwin_arm64 SHA256 (Mac M1/M2)
    "h1:IJKL9012...",  # windows_amd64 SHA256
    "zh:MNOP3456...",  # Signed by HashiCorp (zh: prefix)
  ]
}

provider "registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/kubernetes" {
  version     = "2.35.0"
  constraints = "~> 2.30"
  hashes = [
    "h1:QWER7890...",
    "h1:TYUI1234...",
  ]
}
⚠️ Critical: The Lock File Must Be COMMITTED to Git!

Do NOT add .terraform.lock.hcl to .gitignore. This is a common mistake. The lock file ensures every team member and CI runner uses exactly the same provider binary. Without it, different machines might download different provider versions within the constraint range — leading to subtle, hard-to-debug drift. The .terraform/ directory (cached binaries) should be gitignored; the lock file should NOT.

6.2 The Provider Block — Configuration & Authentication

Provider Block — Basic & Advanced Configurations
# Basic: Single region
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

# Advanced: Multi-region with aliases
provider "aws" {
  alias  = "us_west"
  region = "us-west-2"
}

provider "aws" {
  alias  = "eu_west"
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

# Use specific provider in a resource
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "dr_backup" {
  provider = aws.us_west       # ← Uses the aliased provider
  bucket   = "anihpj-dr-backup"
}

Provider Authentication — The 5 Methods (In Priority Order)

Terraform providers attempt authentication in a specific priority order. Understanding this order is critical for debugging "access denied" errors and for the exam:

PriorityMethodExample (AWS)Security Rating
1st (Highest)Static Credentials in Provider Blockaccess_key = "AKIA..." in provider config🔴 Worst — Never do this!
2ndEnvironment VariablesAWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY🟡 Acceptable for CI/CD
3rdShared Credentials File~/.aws/credentials with [default] or named profile🟡 OK for local dev
4thIAM Role (EC2/EKS)Instance profile / IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)🟢 Best for AWS workloads
5th (Lowest)OIDC FederationTFC → AWS via OIDC (no long-lived credentials!)🟢 Best for TFC/CI pipelines
🚨 NEVER Hardcode Credentials in .tf Files!

Hardcoding access_key and secret_key in provider blocks is the #1 Terraform security anti-pattern. These files get committed to Git → credentials leak. Instead:

  • ✅ Use environment variables (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET)
  • ✅ Use Terraform Cloud workspace variables (marked as Sensitive)
  • ✅ Use OIDC federation for TFC → AWS/Azure/GCP (no static credentials at all)
  • ✅ Use hashicorp/vault provider to dynamically generate short-lived credentials

Provider Aliases — The Complete Reference

Provider Aliases — Multi-Region + Multi-Account Pattern
# Default provider (no alias) — used when no provider is specified
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::111111111111:role/TerraformAdmin"
  }
}

# Named alias for DR region
provider "aws" {
  alias  = "dr"        # ← Alias name: aws.dr
  region = "us-west-2"
  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::222222222222:role/TerraformAdmin"
  }
}

# Named alias for audit/logging account
provider "aws" {
  alias  = "audit"     # ← Alias name: aws.audit
  region = "us-east-1"
  assume_role {
    role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::999999999999:role/TerraformAdmin"
  }
}

# Resources use the appropriate provider
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "primary" {
  # No provider specified → uses DEFAULT provider
  bucket = "anihpj-data-primary"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "dr" {
  provider = aws.dr        # ← Explicit: uses us-west-2 provider
  bucket   = "anihpj-data-dr"
}

resource "aws_cloudtrail" "audit" {
  provider = aws.audit     # ← Explicit: uses audit account provider
  name     = "anihpj-cloudtrail"
}

# 🔑 KEY: provider = aws.alias_name  (not provider = "aws.alias_name")

6.3 Provider Versioning & Constraints — ~> 4.0 Explained

PROVIDER VERSION CONSTRAINTS — What ~> Really Means
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"    ◀── What does this mean?
    }
  }

  "~> 5.0" = ">= 5.0, < 6.0"   (Pessimistic Constraint)

    5.0.0 ✅    5.1.0 ✅    5.99.0 ✅    6.0.0 ❌
    ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
    ">= 5.0, < 5.1"   = "~> 5.0.0" (patch only)
    ">= 5.0, < 6.0"   = "~> 5.0"   (minor updates)
    ">= 5.0"          = ANY 5.x.x+ (dangerous — no upper bound!)
    "= 5.42.0"        = EXACT version (most locked down)

The pessimistic constraint operator (~>) is the most common choice in production because it balances stability with flexibility. It says: "I trust provider maintainers to follow semantic versioning — give me all patches and minor updates, but block the next major version." This is critical because major version bumps introduce breaking changes: resource renames, removed attributes, changed defaults. Without ~>, a terraform init -upgrade could silently pull in a major version that breaks your entire configuration.

⚠️ The "Only Rightmost Component" Rule

~> 5.0 allows 5.1, 5.99 — but NOT 6.0. ~> 5.0.0 allows 5.0.1, 5.0.99 — but NOT 5.1.0. The rightmost specified component is the only one that can increment. Everything to its left is locked. This is the exact rule the exam tests: ~> 1.2.3 means >= 1.2.3, < 1.3.0. Memorize this pattern.

How .terraform.lock.hcl Interacts with Version Constraints
# Your constraints: version = "~> 5.0"  → allows 5.x (not 6.0)
# Lock file records EXACT version: 5.82.0 + checksums per platform

# Team flow:
# terraform init → reads ~> 5.0, checks lock file → downloads EXACTLY 5.82.0
# If checksums differ → ERROR (tampering detected!)
# terraform init -upgrade → checks registry for newest matching ~> 5.0 → updates lock

# Lock file prevents SURPRISE upgrades. -upgrade makes them INTENTIONAL.

6.4 Multiple Provider Configurations — Aliases & Multi-Region

In production, you often need to deploy resources across multiple AWS regions or even multiple cloud providers from a single Terraform configuration. Aliases make this possible.

Multi-Region + Multi-Cloud Example
# Primary (default) AWS provider
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }

# Disaster recovery region
provider "aws" { alias = "dr"; region = "us-west-2" }

# Also deploy to Azure
provider "azurerm" { features {} }

# Use them in resources
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "primary" {
  bucket = "anihpj-assets"       # Uses default provider
}
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "dr" {
  provider = aws.dr              # Uses DR provider
  bucket   = "anihpj-assets-dr"
}

Multi-region deployments are a production necessity, not just disaster recovery. Use provider aliases when: (1) DR/failover — keep data copies in a separate region. (2) Latency optimization — deploy to us-east-1 and eu-west-1 for different user bases. (3) Cross-account architectures — separate AWS accounts per environment, each needing assume_role with its own provider config. (4) Global services — CloudFront (us-east-1 only), Route 53 (global), and IAM (global) may need different regions than your compute. The default provider (no alias) is always your primary — every resource without provider = aws.alias uses it automatically.

6.5 Major Providers — AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Docker, Helm

ProviderPrefixDownloadsManaged Resources
AWSaws4 Billion+1000+ (EC2, VPC, RDS, S3, Lambda...)
Azureazurerm1 Billion+800+ (VM, VNet, AKS, SQL...)
Google Cloudgoogle500 Million+600+ (GCE, GKE, CloudSQL...)
Kuberneteskubernetes200 Million+K8s API resources
Helmhelm100 Million+Helm chart releases
Dockerdocker80 Million+Containers, images, networks, volumes

Each provider has a resource prefix that determines which API it targets. AWS resources start with aws_, Azure uses azurerm_, Google Cloud uses google_. The Kubernetes provider uses kubernetes_ — note that it manages resources inside a cluster (pods, deployments, services), not the cluster itself. To create the cluster, use the cloud-specific provider: aws_eks_cluster, azurerm_kubernetes_cluster, or google_container_cluster. This separation — cluster creation vs cluster content — is a fundamental Terraform pattern you'll use in every production deployment.

☁️ AWS Provider (hashicorp/aws)

The most downloaded provider — 4B+ downloads. Manages 1000+ resource types across 200+ AWS services. From VPC networking to Lambda serverless, RDS databases to EKS clusters, S3 storage to IAM security — if AWS offers it as a service, the AWS provider has a resource for it. The provider is so large it's split into multiple service packages internally, but you interact with it through a single unified provider binary.

☸️ Kubernetes Provider (hashicorp/kubernetes)

Manages resources inside an existing cluster. It talks directly to the K8s API server — you provide kubeconfig credentials. Use it to create Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Ingresses, Namespaces, RBAC rules, and more. Combined with the Helm provider, you can deploy entire application stacks. The provider does NOT create the cluster — that's done by aws_eks_cluster or equivalent.

6.7 Provider Authentication Methods

HOW ANIHPJ AUTHENTICATES TO MULTIPLE PROVIDERS
  AWS:         AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
               (env vars) OR ~/.aws/credentials OR IAM Role

  Docker:      Unix socket (/var/run/docker.sock)
               OR DOCKER_HOST=tcp://...

  Kubernetes:  KUBECONFIG file (~/.kube/config)
               OR in-cluster service account

  Helm:        Same as Kubernetes (uses kubeconfig)

  ⚠️ NEVER hardcode credentials in .tf files!
  ✅ Use env vars, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or TFC variables

6.6 Provider Registry — Finding, Trusting & Pinning Providers

The Terraform Registry (registry.terraform.io) is the central catalog of providers and modules. Every provider has a page showing documentation, version history, and usage examples.

📖 How Provider Resolution Works

source = "hashicorp/aws" resolves to registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws. The format is hostname/namespace/provider. For the public registry, the hostname defaults to registry.terraform.io. For private registries (Terraform Cloud), use the full hostname. Always check a provider's download count and version history before adopting it — this indicates community trust and active maintenance.

Provider Source Address — Decoding the Full Format

The full provider source address format is hostname/namespace/type. Understanding this is essential for private registries and air-gapped environments:

ShorthandExpanded FormWhere It Resolves
hashicorp/awsregistry.terraform.io/hashicorp/awsPublic Terraform Registry
hashicorp/kubernetesregistry.terraform.io/hashicorp/kubernetesPublic Terraform Registry
app.terraform.io/anihpj/custom(No expansion — full hostname given)Private TFC Organization Registry
terraform.example.com/myorg/myprovider(Custom hostname — air-gapped/private)Self-hosted Registry Mirror

Verifying Provider Trustworthiness — Before You init

✅ Trust Signals
  • Official badge: OFFICIAL — Built and signed by HashiCorp
  • Verified badge: VERIFIED — Built by the named organization, signed by HashiCorp
  • High download count: 10M+ downloads indicates widespread production use
  • Recent updates: Latest version released within the last 3 months
  • Documentation quality: Complete resource/sub-resource documentation with examples
⚠️ Red Flags
  • No badge: Community provider with no verification — use with caution
  • Low downloads: <1000 downloads — rarely used, may have bugs
  • Stale: Last release >1 year ago — may not work with current Terraform
  • Sparse docs: Only a README, no detailed resource documentation
  • No GitHub link: Can't inspect source code or report issues

6.8 Building Your Own Provider — When, Why, and How

Terraform providers can be built for any API. If your organization has an internal platform with a REST API, you can build a Terraform provider for it — enabling your team to manage internal services using the same HCL workflow.

💡 When to Build a Custom Provider

✅ Your company has an internal platform with a REST API. ✅ You want to manage SaaS tools not yet covered by existing providers. ✅ You need tighter integration than the HTTP provider offers. The Terraform Plugin Framework (Go SDK) provides scaffolding. Start with: terraform-provider-scaffold repository.

Custom Provider Development — The 4-Layer Architecture

CUSTOM PROVIDER LAYERS — From HCL to Your API
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     TERRAFORM CUSTOM PROVIDER                   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  main.tf ──▶ ┌─────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────┐   │
  │  resource    │  PROVIDER SERVER │    │    YOUR API CLIENT   │   │
  │  "mycloud_   │  (gRPC Protocol) │───▶│    (Go HTTP Client)  │   │
  │  server"     │                 │    │                      │   │
  │  "web" {     │ • Schema (attr) │    │ • POST /servers      │   │
  │    name=".." │ • CRUD funcs    │    │ • GET  /servers/{id} │   │
  │    size=".." │ • State mapping │    │ • PUT  /servers/{id} │   │
  │  }           │ • Plan diff     │    │ • DELETE /servers/id │   │
  │              └─────────────────┘    └──────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  Framework: terraform-plugin-framework (Go)                     │
  │  Scaffold:  github.com/hashicorp/terraform-provider-scaffold    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Minimal Custom Provider — Go Code Skeleton
// main.go — Entry point for a custom Terraform provider
package main

import (
    "context"
    "github.com/hashicorp/terraform-plugin-framework/provider"
    "github.com/hashicorp/terraform-plugin-framework/providerserver"
)

func main() {
    // Serve the provider using Terraform's gRPC plugin protocol
    providerserver.Serve(context.Background(),
        func() provider.Provider {
            return &MyCloudProvider{}  // Your provider implementation
        },
        providerserver.ServeOpts{
            Address: "registry.terraform.io/myorg/mycloud",
        },
    )
}

// Then define:
// 1. Provider struct (with schema for config attrs like api_key, endpoint)
// 2. Resource structs (with schema for each resource's attributes)
// 3. CRUD functions: Create(), Read(), Update(), Delete()
// 4. ImportState() for `terraform import` support

🔑 Ch6 Key Takeaways — Providers Mastered

🔌Adapter Pattern

Provider = Go plugin that translates HCL → cloud API calls. Learn HCL once, deploy to any cloud. 3000+ providers exist.

📥terraform init

7-step lifecycle: parse → resolve source → check version → verify lock → download → verify signature → update lock file.

🔐Auth Priority

5 methods in order: static creds (worst) < env vars < shared credentials < IAM role < OIDC federation (best). Never hardcode!

🔒Lock File

.terraform.lock.hcl pins exact versions + platform checksums. MUST be committed to Git. Prevents provider drift across teams.

🏷️Aliases

provider "aws" { alias = "dr" } → use as provider = aws.dr. Enables multi-region and multi-account deployments.

📦Registry Trust

Look for OFFICIAL/VERIFIED badges, 10M+ downloads, recent releases, and complete docs before adopting a provider.

🧭 How to Choose a Provider from the Registry

The Terraform Registry has 3000+ providers — not all are equal. Here's how to evaluate one before adding it to your project:

🔵 Official BadgePublished by HashiCorp. AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Vault. These are the gold standard.
🟢 Verified BadgePublished by the platform vendor itself (Datadog, GitHub, Cloudflare). Trusted, maintained by the team that owns the API.
🟡 CommunityPublished by third parties. Check: download count (>100K is healthy), last release date (<6 months), GitHub stars, and issue response time.
🔴 ArchivedNo longer maintained. The registry marks these clearly. Migrate away immediately — no security patches, no Terraform version compatibility.
📋 Provider Configuration Checklist for Production
  1. Pin the version — version = "~> 5.0" in required_providers
  2. Commit .terraform.lock.hcl — every team member gets identical binaries
  3. Use OIDC/IAM roles for auth — never static access keys in .tf files
  4. Set default tags at provider level — provider "aws" { default_tags { ... } }
  5. Configure retry/timeout settings — max_retries = 5 for flaky APIs
  6. Use alias for multi-region — separate provider config per region
  7. Cache providers in CI/CD — terraform init -plugin-dir=/cache
  8. Test upgrades in staging first — terraform init -upgrade only after validation

📊 Provider Trust Levels — What to Look For

🔵Officialhashicorp/aws, hashicorp/azurerm, hashicorp/google — 4B+ downloads
🟢Verifieddatadog/datadog, integrations/github — by the API owner
🟡CommunityCheck downloads, release frequency, GitHub activity
🔴ArchivedNo longer maintained — migrate immediately

7.1 AWS Provider Setup — VPC, EC2, RDS, S3, IAM for anihpj

🧠 Exam Focus: Provisioners Are a Last Resort

The Terraform Associate exam WILL test provisioner best practices:

  • Provisioners are NOT idempotent — they run scripts, don't manage state
  • local-exec runs on YOUR machine; remote-exec needs SSH to the resource
  • Failed provisioner → resource is TAINTED → destroyed & recreated next apply
  • Prefer user_data, cloud-init, or Packer golden images over provisioners
  • null_resource + triggers = the standard pattern for running scripts

7.10 Dockerfile for anihpj — Multi-Stage Production Build

Dockerfile — anihpj/jobpost Production-Ready Image
# ═══ STAGE 1: BUILD ═══
FROM python:3.11-slim AS builder
WORKDIR /app
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc libpq-dev && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# ═══ STAGE 2: RUNTIME ═══
FROM python:3.11-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpq-dev curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash anihpj
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /home/anihpj/.local
COPY --chown=anihpj:anihpj . /app
WORKDIR /app; USER anihpj
ENV PATH="/home/anihpj/.local/bin:$PATH"
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost:8000/health/ || exit 1
CMD ["gunicorn", "anihpj.wsgi:application", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000",
     "--workers", "3", "--access-logfile", "-"]

templatefile() Function
# user_data.sh.tpl — Template with variables & conditionals
#!/bin/bash
echo "Deploying ${app_name} in ${environment}"
%{ if enable_ssl }
certbot --nginx -d ${domain}

7.7 Null Provider — Triggering Arbitrary Scripts

The null provider is a special provider that does nothing — it's used as a trigger mechanism for provisioners and to create resources that don't correspond to any real infrastructure.

Null Provider Example — Run DB Migrations
resource "null_resource" "run_migrations" {
  triggers = { db_endpoint = aws_db_instance.pg.address }
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "python manage.py migrate"
  }
}

The null provider is Terraform's escape hatch for arbitrary actions. It creates a resource that doesn't correspond to any real infrastructure — its sole purpose is to run provisioners at specific points in the dependency graph. The triggers map is the key: when any trigger value changes, the null_resource is marked for recreation, causing its provisioners to re-run. Without triggers, the null_resource runs once and never again — which defeats the purpose. Common patterns include: (1) Database migrations after RDS creation (trigger on DB endpoint), (2) Cache warming after Redis deployment, (3) API calls to external systems that have no Terraform provider. The null_resource exists because Terraform is fundamentally about managing infrastructure state, not running scripts — but sometimes you genuinely need both.

⚠️ Null Resource + Provisioner = Fragile

If the provisioner fails, the null_resource is tainted and will be destroyed/recreated on the next apply. This can cascade: a failed migration script taints the null_resource, which triggers re-running the migration, which might fail again. Always test provisioner commands in isolation before embedding them in Terraform. Consider whether a CI/CD pipeline step would be a safer alternative for script execution than a Terraform provisioner.

7.8 Time Provider — Rotation & Time-Based Resources

Time Provider — Rotate Passwords Every 30 Days
resource "time_rotating" "db_password" {
  rotation_days = 30
}
resource "random_password" "db_pass" {
  keepers = { rotation = time_rotating.db_password.id }
  length  = 32
}

The time provider solves a critical problem: time-based rotation of secrets and resources. Without it, passwords set at creation time stay forever — a security anti-pattern. time_rotating generates a new timestamp every rotation_days, which you use as a keepers key on random_password. When the keeper changes, the password regenerates. But here's the crucial detail: changing the password in Terraform does NOT automatically update it in the running application. Your app must be designed to fetch passwords dynamically (from Vault, Secrets Manager, or env vars reloaded on restart). The time provider triggers the rotation — your app handles the consumption. For anihpj/jobpost, combine with aws_secretsmanager_secret_version to push the new password to AWS, then configure Django to read from Secrets Manager at startup.

7.9 TLS Provider — Certificates for anihpj HTTPS

TLS Provider — Self-Signed Dev Certificate
resource "tls_private_key" "anihpj" {
  algorithm = "RSA"; rsa_bits = 4096
}
resource "tls_self_signed_cert" "anihpj" {
  private_key_pem = tls_private_key.anihpj.private_key_pem
  subject { common_name = "anihpj.local" }
  validity_period_hours = 8760  # 1 year
  allowed_uses = ["key_encipherment", "digital_signature"]
}

The TLS provider generates cryptographic keys and certificates within Terraform — no external CA required. It's primarily used for development and internal services where a full PKI isn't justified. For anihpj/jobpost, it creates self-signed certificates for local HTTPS testing. In production, you'd replace these with ACM certificates (AWS) or certificates from a proper CA. The provider supports RSA and ECDSA algorithms, self-signed and CA-signed certificates, and CSR generation. Key use cases: (1) Local dev HTTPS — self-signed cert for Docker/Kind clusters, (2) Internal mTLS — service-to-service encryption within a VPC, (3) SSH key pairs — programmatic generation for EC2 access (though aws_key_pair is better for AWS). Note: self-signed certificates will trigger browser security warnings — they're for development only, not production user-facing endpoints.

📊 Provider Decision Matrix — Which Provider for What?

ProviderBest ForTypical anihpj Use
awsProduction cloudVPC, EC2, RDS, S3, IAM, Route53
dockerLocal dev envDjango + PG + Redis on laptop
kubernetesK8s cluster mgmtDeploy pods, services, ingresses
helmApp deploymentDeploy anihpj via Helm chart
randomPasswords, IDsDB password, unique bucket names
tlsCertificatesSelf-signed certs for dev HTTPS
timeRotationRotate RDS passwords every 30d
nullScripts, triggersRun DB migrations after deploy

📝 Chapter 7 — Terraform Associate Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What is the Docker provider used for in Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

It manages Docker containers, images, networks, and volumes through Terraform. Useful for local development or managing container infrastructure on Docker hosts.

resource "docker_container" "web" {
  name  = "anihpj-web"
  image = docker_image.nginx.latest
  ports { internal = 80; external = 8080 }
}
Explanation

The Docker provider is great for local dev — define your PostgreSQL, Redis, and Django containers as code. But for production, use AWS ECS/EKS providers instead. The Docker provider works with local Docker daemon or remote Docker hosts via TCP/TLS.

Q2
How does the Kubernetes provider authenticate?
Show Answer
Answer

Through kubeconfig files, in-cluster service accounts, or explicit credentials. The provider reads ~/.kube/config by default, or you can specify config_path, host, client_certificate, etc.

Explanation

The K8s provider is often used WITH the AWS provider: Terraform creates the EKS cluster (via AWS provider), then the K8s provider deploys pods/services into that cluster. Use depends_on to ensure the cluster exists before deploying to it.

Q3
What are provisioners and when should you use them?
Show Answer
Answer

Provisioners run scripts on resource creation/destruction. Use as a last resort — prefer user_data, cloud-init, or config management tools. Common types: local-exec, remote-exec, file.

Explanation

The exam emphasizes: provisioners are a LAST RESORT. Terraform can't track what a provisioner script does — if it partially succeeds, state is unaware. Always prefer user_data (EC2), cloud-init, Packer golden images, or config management tools (Ansible, Chef).

Q4
What's the difference between local-exec and remote-exec provisioners?
Show Answer
Answer

local-exec: runs on the machine running Terraform. remote-exec: runs on the provisioned resource (requires SSH/WinRM connection).

Explanation
# Ch7 Q4 — local-exec vs remote-exec

# local-exec: runs WHERE Terraform runs (laptop, CI, TFC agent)
provisioner "local-exec" {
  command = "python manage.py migrate"
  working_dir = "../anihpj"
  environment = { DB_URL = aws_db_instance.pg.endpoint }
}

# remote-exec: runs ON the created resource (needs SSH)
provisioner "remote-exec" {
  inline = ["sudo apt update", "sudo apt install -y nginx"]
  connection { host = self.public_ip; type = "ssh"; user = "ubuntu" }
}

local-exec doesn't need SSH. remote-exec requires SSH connectivity. The exam will test this distinction.

Q5
What happens if a provisioner fails?
Show Answer
Answer

The resource is marked as tainted — it will be destroyed and recreated on the next terraform apply. Use on_failure = continue to allow the resource to persist despite provisioner failure.

Explanation

By default, a failed provisioner TAINTS the resource → destroyed and recreated on next apply. This can cause data loss. Use on_failure = continue when the provisioner is optional (e.g., sending a notification). The exam: "What happens when a provisioner fails?" → resource is tainted.

Q6
How do you pass values from a resource to a provisioner script?
Show Answer
Answer

Use self to reference the resource's attributes: self.public_ip. For local-exec, pass via environment map or interpolate directly in the command string.

Explanation

self is the magic variable inside provisioners — it refers to the parent resource. self.public_ip, self.private_key_pem, etc. For local-exec use the environment map: environment = { DB_HOST = self.address }. The script reads $DB_HOST.

Q7
What is the null_resource and when is it useful?
Show Answer
Answer

null_resource is a do-nothing resource that runs provisioners. Use it when you need to run a script but don't need a real cloud resource. Its triggers map controls when it re-runs.

Explanation

null_resource is the standard pattern for "run this script when X changes." Example: run database migrations whenever the DB endpoint or app version changes. The triggers act like a hash — if any trigger value changes, the null_resource is recreated (re-running its provisioners).

Q8
How do you provision an EC2 instance with a startup script WITHOUT using provisioners?
Show Answer
Answer

Use the user_data argument with templatefile(). This is the preferred approach — it runs at boot time without SSH, is idempotent, and doesn't require Terraform to maintain a connection.

Explanation

user_data is the AWS-native way to bootstrap instances. It runs once at launch, doesn't need SSH, and works at scale. Combined with templatefile(), you can inject dynamic values. This is the PREFERRED approach — provisioners are for when user_data can't do what you need.

Q9
What does the triggers argument in null_resource do?
Show Answer
Answer

It defines when to re-run the null_resource's provisioners. When any trigger value changes, the resource is recreated (re-running the provisioner). Example: triggers = { app_version = var.version }

Explanation

Triggers act as a fingerprint — when any trigger value changes, the null_resource is marked for recreation. This is how you make provisioners idempotent: tie triggers to the values your script depends on. If nothing changed, the script doesn't re-run.

Q10
Can provisioners be used with data sources?
Show Answer
Answer

No. Provisioners only work with resource blocks, not data sources. Data sources are read-only and don't support creation/destruction lifecycle hooks.

Explanation

Data sources are pure reads — they have no create/update/delete lifecycle, so provisioners (which hook into lifecycle events) have nothing to hook into. If you need to run a script based on a data source query, use null_resource with a trigger that depends on the data source.

🔑 Ch7 Key Takeaways — Provisioning anihpj/jobpost on AWS

☁️AWS Stack

VPC → Subnets → EKS/EC2 → RDS → S3 → IAM → Route53. Every resource defined as code. Full infrastructure in one terraform apply.

🐳Docker Provider

Local dev: docker_container + docker_image + docker_network. Full Django+PG+Redis stack on laptop with one command. Zero AWS cost for dev.

☸️K8s Provider

Deploy pods, services, ingresses AFTER EKS is created. Use depends_on to ensure cluster exists. Authenticate via kubeconfig or IRSA.

📦ECR + Docker

Build image locally → push to ECR → K8s pulls from private registry. docker_registry_image + ecr_repository. IAM auth for K8s → ECR pull.

⚠️Provisioners

Last resort only. Failed provisioner = tainted resource. Prefer user_data, cloud-init, Packer images. null_resource + triggers for script orchestration.

🔐IAM + Security

IRSA for K8s → AWS permissions. Security groups: only necessary ports. Secrets in AWS Secrets Manager, never in .tf files. Least privilege principle.

🐳 Docker Provider

Best for: Local dev, CI testing
Not for: Production deployments

Auth: Local Docker socket (no config needed)

☸️ Kubernetes Provider

Best for: Deploying to existing clusters
Not for: Creating EKS/GKE/AKS clusters

📦 Helm Provider

Best for: Pre-packaged apps (nginx, prometheus)
Not for: Custom microservices
Key resources: helm_release

Tip: wait = true ensures pods are ready

Chapter 8: Resources Deep Dive 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 8: Resources Deep Dive — Mastering Terraform's Core Construct

Resources are the heart of Terraform. Every cloud component you manage — VPCs, instances, databases, load balancers — is defined as a resource block. This chapter goes deep into resource syntax, dependencies, lifecycle rules, meta-arguments, and the critical decisions about when Terraform updates in-place vs destroys and recreates.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~2 hours 🧱 Resources 🎯 Critical

8.1 Resource Syntax — Everything You Can Configure

Every resource block follows the same pattern: resource "type" "name" { arguments }. Understanding this syntax deeply means you can work with ANY resource from ANY provider.

Resource Syntax — Complete Reference
resource "aws_instance" "anihpj_web" {   # ← type.name = unique address
  # Required arguments (provider-specific)
  ami           = "ami-0c55b159cbfafe1f0"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  
  # Optional arguments
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public[0].id
  key_name      = var.ssh_key_name
  
  # Meta-arguments (available on ALL resources)
  count         = 3              # Create N copies
  depends_on    = [aws_s3_bucket.assets]  # Explicit dependency
  provider      = aws.us_west    # Non-default provider
  
  # Nested blocks
  root_block_device { volume_size = 20 }
  
  # Lifecycle
  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
    ignore_changes = [ami]       # Don't replace on AMI change
  }
}

8.2 Resource Dependencies — Implicit vs Explicit

IMPLICIT vs EXPLICIT DEPENDENCIES
  IMPLICIT (Terraform figures it out from references):
  resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" }
  resource "aws_subnet" "public" {
    vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id  ◀── Terraform sees this & KNOWS subnet
  }                                depends on VPC. Creates VPC FIRST.

  EXPLICIT (You tell Terraform — use only when no reference exists):
  resource "null_resource" "upload_files" {
    depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket.assets]  ◀── No reference to bucket
    provisioner "local-exec" {                in body, so TF wouldn't
      command = "aws s3 sync ./static s3://anihpj-assets/"  know.
    }                               depends_on fixes this.
  }

Deep Dive: How Terraform Builds the Dependency Graph

Terraform doesn't just "figure it out" — it builds a formal Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of all resources. This is one of the most elegant parts of Terraform's architecture:

DEPENDENCY GRAPH RESOLUTION — How Terraform Orders Operations
1
Parse all .tf files
Every resource, data source, variable, and output is read. Terraform builds an AST (Abstract Syntax Tree).
→
2
Extract References
Every aws_vpc.main.id reference is detected. Terraform traces: "This subnet references VPC main → VPC must exist first."
→
3
Build Dependency Graph
Nodes = resources; Edges = "must exist before." Uses topological sort to find valid creation orders.
→
4
Detect Parallelism
Resources with NO edges between them can be created in PARALLEL (up to -parallelism=N, default 10).
→
5
Execute in Waves
Wave 1: VPC, IAM roles (no dependencies). Wave 2: Subnets, gateways (depend on VPC). Wave 3: EC2, RDS (depend on subnets + security groups).
📖 When to Use depends_on — The Rule

Use depends_on ONLY when Terraform cannot detect the dependency through interpolation. Examples of when it's needed:

  • Provisioners accessing resources: A local-exec uploads to S3, but the bucket name is hardcoded (not interpolated) → Terraform doesn't know the dependency
  • Side effects: Resource A creates something that Resource B's API checks for, but B doesn't reference A's attributes
  • Cross-workspace ordering: Workspace B must wait for Workspace A (handled by run triggers, not depends_on)

99% of the time, implicit dependencies via interpolation are sufficient and preferred. Excessive depends_on indicates you're not using interpolation properly.

Visualizing the Dependency Graph — terraform graph

Generate and Visualize the Dependency Graph
# Generate DOT-format graph
terraform graph > graph.dot

# Visualize (requires Graphviz: brew install graphviz / apt install graphviz)
dot -Tpng graph.dot -o graph.png

# The graph shows:
# ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐
# │ aws_vpc  │────▶│aws_subnet│────▶│aws_inst. │
# │  .main   │     │ .public  │     │  web     │
# └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────┘
# Arrows point FROM dependency TO dependent

8.3 Resource Meta-Arguments — count, for_each, lifecycle, provider

Meta-arguments are special arguments available on EVERY resource block. They control how many instances are created, dependencies, and lifecycle behavior.

count vs for_each — The Definitive Comparison (Exam Critical!)

This is one of the MOST tested topics on the exam. Understanding when to use count vs for_each is essential:

Criterioncountfor_each
InputInteger: count = 3Map or Set of strings
Instance AddressIndex: aws_instance.web[0], web[1]Key: aws_instance.web["app"], web["db"]
Adding an Item Mid-list🔴 DESTROYS and RECREATES everything after insertion point!🟢 Only creates the new item — no changes to existing
Removing an Item Mid-list🔴 Shifts ALL subsequent indexes → mass destruction🟢 Only destroys the removed item
Best ForIdentical, stateless replicas (worker nodes)Named, distinctly configured resources (databases, queues)
Current Valuecount.index (0, 1, 2...)each.key + each.value
count vs for_each — Side-by-Side Comparison
# ❌ COUNT: Fragile with insertions/deletions
variable "subnet_cidrs" {
  type    = list(string)
  default = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]
}
resource "aws_subnet" "by_count" {
  count      = length(var.subnet_cidrs)
  cidr_block = var.subnet_cidrs[count.index]
  # If you insert "10.0.99.0/24" at index 0:
  # subnet[0] DESTROYED (was 10.0.1.0, now 10.0.99.0)
  # subnet[1] DESTROYED (was 10.0.2.0, now 10.0.1.0)  ← CASCADING!
  # subnet[2] DESTROYED (was 10.0.3.0, now 10.0.2.0)
  # subnet[3] CREATED   (new 10.0.3.0)
}

# ✅ FOR_EACH: Stable — keys are the identity
variable "subnet_cidrs" {
  type = map(string)
  default = {
    public-a  = "10.0.1.0/24"
    public-b  = "10.0.2.0/24"
    private-a = "10.0.3.0/24"
  }
}
resource "aws_subnet" "by_key" {
  for_each   = var.subnet_cidrs
  cidr_block = each.value
  tags       = { Name = each.key }
  # Adding new key "public-c": ONLY creates the new subnet
  # Removing key "public-a": ONLY destroys that subnet
  # Existing subnets are UNTOUCHED!
}
⚠️ The count Index Problem — Exam Will Test This!

If you have count = 3 and you remove index 0 from your list, ALL resources get new indexes. Terraform sees this as: "Destroy web[0], web[1], web[2] → Create web[0], web[1]." In production, this means unnecessary downtime. Use for_each with maps to keep resource identities stable. The exam question: "A developer adds a new element to the beginning of a list used with count. What happens?" → All resources after the insertion point are destroyed and recreated.

Meta-Arguments in Action
# count — Create N identical resources
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count         = 3                    # Creates web[0], web[1], web[2]
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  tags = { Name = "web-${count.index}" }  # count.index = 0, 1, 2
}

# for_each — Create from a map (keys survive additions/removals)
resource "aws_instance" "app" {
  for_each      = { web="t3.medium", worker="t3.small" }
  instance_type = each.value           # "t3.medium", "t3.small"
  tags = { Name = each.key }           # "web", "worker"
}

# lifecycle — Control create/destroy behavior
resource "aws_db_instance" "prod_db" {
  # ... config ...
  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true             # Block accidental deletion
    ignore_changes  = [engine_version] # Don't reset minor version upgrades
  }
}

8.4 Lifecycle Rules — create_before_destroy, prevent_destroy, ignore_changes

THE 4 LIFECYCLE META-ARGUMENTS
  create_before_destroy = true    ← Create NEW resource FIRST, then destroy old
                                    ✅ Zero-downtime updates!
  prevent_destroy       = true    ← BLOCK accidental deletion
                                    ❌ terraform destroy REFUSES
  ignore_changes        = [...]   ← Ignore specific attribute changes
                                    e.g., ignore autoscaling adjustments
  replace_triggered_by  = [...]   ← Force recreate when attribute changes
                                    e.g., recreate when AMI changes

  create_before_destroy (avoid downtime):
  WITHOUT: Destroy old EC2 → (downtime!) → Create new EC2
  WITH:    Create new EC2 → (both running) → Destroy old EC2
           ✅ Zero downtime!  ⚠️ Need enough quota for 2x resources

Real-World Lifecycle Patterns — When to Use Each

🔄 create_before_destroy = true

Use when: You need zero-downtime for stateful resources (EC2 with EBS, RDS instances, ELB). New resource creates and passes health checks BEFORE old is destroyed.

Pitfall: You need double the resource quota (2 instances briefly exist). If you're at quota limit, apply will FAIL.

Example: Changing EC2 instance type — new instance of new type starts, traffic shifts, old instance terminates. Users see zero interruption.

🛡️ prevent_destroy = true

Use when: Protecting critical resources from accidental deletion (production databases, DNS zones, S3 buckets with data).

Pitfall: terraform destroy will FAIL with an error. Must remove prevent_destroy first, then destroy. This is BY DESIGN — a safety mechanism.

Example: Production RDS database — if someone changes the identifier (causing recreate), Terraform says "NO — this would destroy production data."

👁️ ignore_changes = [...]

Use when: An external process modifies a resource attribute, and you don't want Terraform to "fix" it back. Common for auto-scaling groups, tags added by AWS, minor RDS version upgrades.

Pitfall: Terraform won't detect drift in those attributes. If the external change breaks something, Terraform won't help you.

Example: ignore_changes = [desired_count] on ECS service — allows auto-scaling to adjust count without Terraform resetting it.

🔁 replace_triggered_by = [...]

Use when: You want to force recreation when a referenced attribute changes, even if the provider could technically update in-place. Manual control over the replace/update decision.

Pitfall: Overuse causes unnecessary downtime. Only use when in-place update would leave the resource in a bad state.

Example: Recreate EC2 when the launch template changes — ensures the instance gets the new bootstrap config.

⚠️ Lifecycle Rules Do NOT Prevent Destruction from count/for_each Changes

prevent_destroy = true only blocks terraform destroy and attribute changes that trigger recreation. It does NOT protect against removing a resource by reducing count or removing a key from for_each. The exam may test this distinction. If you set count = 0, the resource is removed regardless of prevent_destroy.

8.5 Tainted Resources — terraform taint

Tainting marks a resource for destruction and recreation on the next terraform apply. Use it when a resource is in a bad state and you want a fresh replacement.

Using taint to Force Recreation
$ terraform taint aws_instance.anihpj_web[0]
Resource aws_instance.anihpj_web[0] is marked as tainted.

# Next terraform apply:
# 1. DESTROY the tainted resource
# 2. CREATE a brand new replacement

$ terraform untaint aws_instance.anihpj_web[0]  # Remove taint if mistake
$ terraform apply  # Now nothing happens to web[0]

8.8 Provisioners — The "Last Resort" Pattern

Provisioners let you run scripts during resource creation or destruction. But HashiCorp recommends using them only as a last resort — they break Terraform's declarative model and can't track what they've done.

PROVISIONER HIERARCHY — Best to Worst
  ✅ BEST: Provider-native features (user_data, cloud-init)
  ✅ GOOD: Pre-baked AMI / Docker image with everything needed
  ⚠️ OK:   Configuration management (Ansible AFTER Terraform)
  🔴 LAST: Terraform provisioners (local-exec, remote-exec)

  local-exec (runs on YOUR machine):
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "echo ${self.public_ip} >> inventory.ini"
  }
  ⚠️ Runs on Terraform host, NOT the resource
  ❌ Not captured in state — if fails, Terraform may not know

  remote-exec (runs ON the resource via SSH):
  provisioner "remote-exec" {
    inline = ["sudo apt-get update", "sudo apt-get install -y nginx"]
  }
  ⚠️ Requires SSH access; can't track provisioner state

8.6 Resource Targeting — Apply to Specific Resources Only

The -target flag limits plan, apply, or destroy to specific resources. Use only for debugging — never in production workflows.

Resource Targeting
$ terraform plan -target=aws_instance.anihpj_web[0]
# Only shows web[0] — everything else hidden
# ⚠️ Breaks the dependency graph! Use only for recovery.

8.7 Timeouts — Custom Operation Time Limits

Resource Timeouts
resource "aws_db_instance" "anihpj_db" {
  engine = "postgres"; instance_class = "db.t3.medium"
  timeouts {
    create = "40m"   # Default 20min; RDS can take longer
    update = "80m"   # Multi-AZ conversion can be SLOW
    delete = "60m"   # Final snapshot takes time
  }
}

8.9 Connection Block — SSH/WinRM for Remote Provisioners

Connection blocks configure how Terraform connects to a resource for remote-exec and file provisioners.

Connection Block
connection {
  type        = "ssh"
  user        = "ec2-user"
  private_key = file("~/.ssh/anihpj.pem")
  host        = self.public_ip
}

8.10 Resource Replacement vs Update — When Terraform Destroys

Change MadeActionPlan Symbol
Change tagsUpdate in-place~
Change instance_typeRecreate 🔄-/+
Change AMIRecreate 🔄-/+
Change security groupUpdate in-place~
Change subnetRecreate 🔄-/+
Change volume size (up)Update in-place~
Change volume size (down)Recreate 🔄-/+
REPLACE vs UPDATE — The Decision Algorithm (Exam Critical!)
  YOU CHANGE AN ATTRIBUTE IN .tf
           │
           ▼
  ┌─────────────────────┐
  │ Can provider update │
  │ this in-place?      │
  └─────────┬───────────┘
            │
    ┌───────┴───────┐
    │               │
    ▼ YES           ▼ NO
 ┌────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
 │ UPDATE │    │ DESTROY +    │
 │ IN-PLACE│   │ RECREATE     │
 │ ~ tags │    │ -/+ AMI      │
 │ ~ sg   │    │ -/+ subnet   │
 └────────┘    │ -/+ vol down │
               └──────┬───────┘
                      │
                      ▼
               ┌──────────────────┐
               │ lifecycle {       │
               │   create_before_  │
               │   destroy = true  │
               │ }                 │
               │ TRUE: New first → │
               │   then delete old │
               │ FALSE: Delete old │
               │   first → new     │
               └──────────────────┘
⚠️ Exam Trap: AMI change = DESTROY/RECREATE

EC2 instances do NOT support in-place AMI updates. Changing the AMI ID in your resource block causes Terraform to destroy the old instance and create a new one. This means DOWNTIME unless you use create_before_destroy. The exam WILL test this.

8.11 Moved Blocks — Refactoring Resources Without Destruction

When you rename a resource or move it into a module, Terraform normally sees it as "destroy old, create new" — which means DOWNTIME. moved blocks (introduced in Terraform 1.1) tell Terraform: "This resource didn't get deleted — it just got renamed." No destroy, no recreate, just a state pointer update.

moved Block — Safe Resource Renaming
# BEFORE: Resource named "web"
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami = "ami-123"
}

# AFTER: Renamed to "main" + added moved block
moved {
  from = aws_instance.web       # Old address
  to   = aws_instance.main      # New address
}

resource "aws_instance" "main" {
  ami = "ami-123"
}
# Result: terraform plan shows "0 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy"
# ✅ State pointer updated — NO infrastructure change!

# Moving a resource INTO a module:
moved {
  from = aws_instance.legacy_web
  to   = module.compute.aws_instance.web
}

# Moving FROM a module:
moved {
  from = module.old_vpc.aws_vpc.main
  to   = aws_vpc.main
}
💡 moved Block Best Practices
  • Keep moved blocks temporarily — After all team members have run terraform apply with the moved block, you can remove it. The state has already been updated.
  • One moved block per move — Each moved block handles exactly one resource relocation.
  • Works across modules — Can move resources into or out of modules seamlessly.
  • Exam tip: terraform plan with a moved block shows "0 to add, 0 to destroy" — the resource is simply relabeled in state.

8.12 Import Blocks — Declarative Resource Import (Terraform 1.5+)

Traditionally, importing existing resources required the CLI command terraform import ADDRESS ID. import blocks (introduced in Terraform 1.5) let you declare imports in your .tf files — making imports reviewable, version-controlled, and part of your IaC workflow.

import Block — Declarative vs CLI import
# OLD WAY: CLI import (manual, not version-controlled)
# $ terraform import aws_vpc.existing vpc-abc12345

# NEW WAY: import block (declarative, in .tf files!)
import {
  to = aws_vpc.existing           # Resource address in your config
  id = "vpc-abc12345"             # Real-world resource ID
}

resource "aws_vpc" "existing" {
  # After terraform plan, run terraform apply
  # Terraform reads the real VPC and fills in these values
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"      # You provide what you know
  # Missing attributes are imported from the real resource
}

# After import, run: terraform plan
# Terraform generates the full resource config based on real-world state
# Then: terraform apply to import
📖 import Block vs. terraform import CLI
Featureimport block (1.5+)terraform import CLI
Declared in.tf files (version-controlled)Terminal only (not tracked)
Generates config?✅ Yes — plan shows full resource config❌ Must write config manually
Reviewable?✅ PR reviewable❌ No review mechanism
Bulk import?✅ Multiple import blocks in one apply❌ One resource at a time

8.13 Check Blocks — Validating Infrastructure Post-Apply

check blocks (introduced in Terraform 1.5) validate that your infrastructure is ACTUALLY in the expected state AFTER apply. Unlike precondition/postcondition which run during planning, check blocks run against real infrastructure — they catch real-world issues like "the load balancer health check is failing" or "the DNS record didn't propagate."

check Block — Post-Apply Infrastructure Validation
check "health_check" {
  # Assertions that run AFTER apply, against real infrastructure
  assert {
    condition     = data.http.lb_health.status_code == 200
    error_message = "Load balancer health check failed! Status: ${data.http.lb_health.status_code}"
  }

  assert {
    condition     = aws_db_instance.main.status == "available"
    error_message = "Database is not available! Status: ${aws_db_instance.main.status}"
  }
}

data "http" "lb_health" {
  url = "http://${aws_lb.main.dns_name}/health"
}

# Key difference from precondition/postcondition:
# precondition  → Runs during PLAN, checks CONFIGURATION values
# postcondition → Runs during PLAN, checks PLANNED state
# check         → Runs AFTER apply, checks REAL infrastructure!
📋 precondition

Runs: During plan
Validates: Input values
Example: "Variable must be a valid CIDR"

📤 postcondition

Runs: During plan
Validates: Planned output
Example: "S3 bucket name must be unique"

✅ check

Runs: After apply
Validates: Real infrastructure
Example: "Load balancer returns 200 OK"

8.14 Debugging Tools — terraform console, TF_LOG, -replace

terraform console — Interactive Expression Testing

terraform console opens an interactive REPL where you can test expressions, functions, and interpolations against your REAL state — without modifying anything.

terraform console Examples
$ terraform console
> var.environment
"production"
> lookup(var.instance_types, "prod", "t3.micro")
"t3.large"
> [for s in aws_subnet.public : s.cidr_block]
["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]
> cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 5)
"10.0.5.0/24"
> exit  # or Ctrl+D

TF_LOG — Debugging Terraform Internals

When Terraform behaves unexpectedly, enable detailed logging to see exactly what's happening under the hood:

TF_LOG Environment Variables
# Enable logging (TRACE, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR)
export TF_LOG=DEBUG              # Shows provider API calls, state operations
export TF_LOG=TRACE              # Everything — including HTTP request/response bodies

# Log to a file (instead of stderr)
export TF_LOG_PATH=./terraform.log

# Only log specific subsystems:
export TF_LOG=DEBUG
export TF_LOG_CORE=TRACE         # Terraform core operations
export TF_LOG_PROVIDER=DEBUG     # Provider-specific operations

# Common debugging workflow:
export TF_LOG=DEBUG TF_LOG_PATH=./debug.log
terraform plan 2>&1 | tee plan-output.txt
# Review debug.log for detailed provider API calls, state reads, etc.

-replace Flag — Force Resource Recreation

The -replace flag (Terraform 1.0+, replacing deprecated terraform taint) forces a specific resource to be destroyed and recreated on the next apply:

-replace vs taint
# MODERN: -replace flag (preferred since Terraform 1.0)
terraform plan -replace=aws_instance.web[0]
terraform apply -replace=aws_instance.web[0]

# LEGACY: terraform taint (still works but deprecated)
terraform taint aws_instance.web[0]
terraform apply    # Destroys + recreates web[0]

# The -replace flag is BETTER because:
# ✅ Plan shows exactly what will happen
# ✅ One-step operation (no separate taint + apply)
# ✅ More explicit intent in CI/CD pipelines

8.15 Removed Blocks — Safely Removing Resources from State (Terraform 1.7+)

When you delete a resource block from your .tf files, Terraform plans to destroy the real resource. But what if you want to stop managing a resource with Terraform WITHOUT destroying it? Enter the removed block (Terraform 1.7+) — it tells Terraform: "Remove this from state, but DON'T destroy the actual infrastructure."

removed Block — Stop Managing Without Destroying
# SCENARIO: You moved an S3 bucket to another team's management.
# You want Terraform to forget about it, but NOT delete the bucket.

# Step 1: Delete the resource block from your .tf files
# resource "aws_s3_bucket" "legacy_assets" { ... }  ← DELETED

# Step 2: Add a removed block to tell Terraform: "Forget, don't destroy"
removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy_assets
  # Optional: lifecycle to destroy the resource
  # lifecycle {
  #   destroy = false  # default — DON'T destroy the real resource
  # }
}

# Step 3: terraform apply
# Result: Resource removed from state file.
# The REAL S3 bucket still exists — just no longer managed by Terraform.

# Alternative: Destroy AND remove (if you want both)
removed {
  from = aws_instance.old_server
  lifecycle {
    destroy = true  # Destroy the real resource AND remove from state
  }
}
💡 removed vs. terraform state rm
MethodVersion Controlled?Reviewable?Best For
removed block✅ Yes — in .tf files✅ PR reviewableTeam workflows, production changes
terraform state rm❌ CLI only❌ No traceQuick cleanup, debugging

8.16 terraform_data — Built-in Managed Resource (Replaces null_resource)

terraform_data is a built-in resource type (Terraform 1.4+) that stores values and triggers operations WITHOUT creating real infrastructure. It replaces the null_resource pattern for most use cases — no provider download needed, works out of the box, and supports replace_triggered_by for clean dependency management.

terraform_data — Replace null_resource
# OLD WAY: null_resource (requires null provider download)
resource "null_resource" "migrate_db" {
  triggers = {
    db_endpoint = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint
  }
  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = "python manage.py migrate"
  }
}

# NEW WAY: terraform_data (built-in, no provider needed!)
resource "terraform_data" "migrate_db" {
  # triggers_replacement forces recreation when any value changes
  triggers_replace = {
    db_endpoint = aws_db_instance.main.endpoint
    app_version = var.app_version
  }

  # input stores arbitrary data (optional)
  input = {
    migration_command = "python manage.py migrate"
  }

  provisioner "local-exec" {
    command = self.input.migration_command
  }
}

# Use with replace_triggered_by in OTHER resources:
resource "aws_ecs_service" "jobpost" {
  # Force ECS service redeployment when migration finishes
  lifecycle {
    replace_triggered_by = [
      terraform_data.migrate_db.id
    ]
  }
}
✅ When to Use terraform_data
  • Running provisioners (migrations, seed data, API calls)
  • Storing computed values for other resources to reference
  • Triggering resource replacement via replace_triggered_by
  • Any scenario where you previously used null_resource
❌ When NOT to Use
  • Managing real cloud resources (use provider resources)
  • Storing secrets (use Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or sensitive variables)
  • Replacing genuine infrastructure — terraform_data creates nothing real

8.17 Lifecycle action_trigger — Invoking Provider Actions Automatically

action_trigger (Terraform 1.9+) lets you invoke provider-defined actions at specific lifecycle events — before or after create/update. Think of it as "Terraform-native provisioners" that are provider-aware and tracked in state. Unlike generic provisioners, actions are defined by the provider and can be idempotent.

action_trigger — Provider-Native Lifecycle Hooks
resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  ami           = "ami-abc123"
  instance_type = "t3.micro"

  lifecycle {
    action_trigger {
      events    = [after_create]        # When: after resource is created
      condition = var.enable_provision  # If: only when this is true
      actions   = [action.ansible_playbook.provision]  # What: run this
    }

    action_trigger {
      events  = [before_update]         # When: before in-place update
      actions = [action.health_check.run]  # What: verify before proceeding
    }
  }
}

# Define the action (provider-specific)
action "ansible_playbook" "provision" {
  playbook = "./playbooks/web-setup.yml"
  # Provider handles execution, retries, and state tracking
}

# Key advantages over provisioners:
# ✅ Provider-aware — understands the resource type
# ✅ State-tracked — Terraform knows if action succeeded
# ✅ Idempotent — provider handles re-run safety
# ✅ Better error handling — provider-specific error recovery
📖 action_trigger vs provisioners

Provisioners (local-exec, remote-exec, file) are generic scripts — Terraform has no idea what they do. action_trigger invokes provider-defined actions that Terraform understands. For the exam, know that action_trigger is the modern, preferred alternative to provisioners when the provider supports it. Events: before_create, after_create, before_update, after_update.

📝 Chapter 8 — Terraform Associate Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What is the resource address format in Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

resource_type.resource_name — e.g., aws_instance.web. For modules: module.name.resource_type.resource_name. This address is used in terraform state commands, -target, and depends_on.

Explanation

Format: resource_type.name[INDEX]. Module: module.NAME.resource_type.name. Used everywhere: state commands, -target flag, depends_on, moved blocks. The address uniquely identifies each resource.

Q2
What does depends_on do and when is it necessary?
Show Answer
Answer

It creates an explicit dependency between resources. Only needed when Terraform can't infer the dependency from references — typically for IAM policies, null_resources, or when dependencies are hidden inside provisioners.

depends_on = [aws_iam_role_policy.ecs_policy]  # Explicit ordering
Explanation

Terraform builds an implicit dependency graph from references. depends_on is ONLY needed when Terraform can't infer the dependency — typically IAM policies (referenced by ARN string, not resource reference), null_resources, or provisioner-internal dependencies. Overusing it is an anti-pattern.

Q3
What are the three lifecycle meta-arguments?
Show Answer
Answer

create_before_destroy — new resource created first, then old deleted. prevent_destroy — blocks accidental deletion (terraform destroy fails). ignore_changes — ignores external changes to specified attributes.

Explanation

These three lifecycle rules control resource replacement behavior. create_before_destroy is critical for zero-downtime. prevent_destroy protects stateful resources (databases!). ignore_changes handles external modifications. The exam will test all three.

Q4
When would you use create_before_destroy?
Show Answer
Answer

For zero-downtime deployments — when you need the new resource running before the old one is destroyed. Critical for stateful resources like databases, or when an EC2 instance's AMI changes.

Explanation

Without create_before_destroy, Terraform deletes the old resource FIRST, then creates the new one — causing downtime. With it, the new resource is created while the old one still runs. Once the new one is ready, the old is destroyed. Requires resources to have unique names (append random suffix).

Q5
What does ignore_changes do? Give a real example.
Show Answer
Answer

It tells Terraform to ignore external modifications to specific attributes. Example: ignore_changes = [tags, tags_all] — if someone adds a tag in the AWS console, Terraform won't remove it on the next apply.

Explanation

Common use: ignore_changes = [ami, user_data] on an ASG launch template — if someone updates the AMI outside Terraform, don't revert it. Another: ignore_changes = [tags, tags_all] when cloud services auto-add tags. The exam: "How do you prevent Terraform from overwriting manual changes?" → ignore_changes.

Q6
What is taint and what replaced it?
Show Answer
Answer

terraform taint ADDR marks a resource for recreation on next apply. Deprecated in TF 1.5+ — use terraform apply -replace=ADDR instead. The -replace flag is safer because it doesn't modify state until apply succeeds.

# Example usage:
terraform apply -auto-approve tfplan

terraform taint modifies state immediately (marks resource as "tainted"). If the subsequent apply fails, state is already changed. -replace doesn't touch state until the replacement succeeds — much safer. The exam may ask about the deprecated taint command.

Q7
How does Terraform determine the order to create/destroy resources?
Show Answer
Answer

It builds a dependency graph automatically from resource references. Resources with dependencies wait. Destruction happens in reverse order. depends_on adds explicit edges to the graph.

Explanation

Terraform builds a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). Each resource reference (like aws_vpc.main.id) creates an edge. Creation = topological order (dependencies first). Destruction = reverse topological order. Resources at the same level are created in parallel (up to -parallelism limit).

Q8
What is a resource's id attribute?
Show Answer
Answer

Every resource has an id — the provider's unique identifier for that resource. For AWS: i-0c55b159cbfafe1f0 (EC2), vpc-12345 (VPC). It's set by the provider after creation and stored in state.

Explanation

The id is the bridge between Terraform and the cloud provider. Terraform uses the address (aws_instance.web) internally, but the provider uses the id (i-0c55b159) for API calls. The state file maps one to the other. All resources have an id even if you don't explicitly set it.

Q9
What happens when you change a resource's name in .tf?
Show Answer
Answer

Terraform sees it as delete old + create new (destroy & recreate), NOT a rename. Use terraform state mv old_name new_name to rename without destroying the resource.

# Example usage:
terraform state list

Resource names are part of the resource ADDRESS, not the resource itself. Changing the name = new address = Terraform thinks old resource should be deleted and a new one created. state mv just updates the address mapping in state — no API calls, no downtime. Common exam trap.

Q10
What is the difference between count and for_each applied to resources?
Show Answer
Answer

count = 3 creates resources name[0], name[1], name[2] — if you remove [1], [2] shifts down and gets destroyed. for_each uses stable keys from a map/set — removing one key only destroys that one resource.

Explanation

This is the single most tested resource meta-argument distinction. With count, index values determine resource identity — changing the list causes cascading destroys. With for_each, the map key IS the identity — add/remove freely without affecting other resources. The exam will ask: "Which should you use?" → for_each for most cases.

🔑 Ch8 Key Takeaways — Resources Mastered

📝Resource Address

resource_type.name[index]. Module: module.NAME.type.name. Used in state commands, -target, depends_on, moved blocks.

🔗Dependency Graph

Terraform builds a DAG. Implicit deps via interpolation (99% of cases). Explicit depends_on only when no interpolation reference exists.

🔢count vs for_each

count uses indexes (fragile). for_each uses stable keys (robust). Insertion in a count list = cascading destruction. Exam favorite!

🔄Lifecycle

4 rules: create_before_destroy (zero-downtime), prevent_destroy (safety lock), ignore_changes (external mgmt), replace_triggered_by (force recreate).

🏷️Tainting

terraform taint marks for destroy+recreate on next apply. untaint reverses. Resource is replaced regardless of config changes.

⚠️Update vs Replace

AMI change = destroy+recreate (exam trap!). Tags/SG = update in-place. check plan symbols: ~ (update), -/+ (replace), + (create), - (destroy).

📝 Chapter 6 — Terraform Associate Practice Questions (10 Questions)

Q1
What is a Terraform provider and how does it work?
Show Answer
Answer

A provider is a Go binary plugin that translates HCL resource declarations into cloud platform API calls. It is downloaded during terraform init.

# Example usage:
terraform init -upgrade

Providers are the adapter layer between Terraform Core and cloud APIs. Each provider (~100-500MB Go binary) knows the specific API of its target platform. When you write resource "aws_vpc" "main" {}, the AWS provider translates that into a CreateVpc API call. Providers handle authentication, retries, error handling, and state mapping. They're stored in .terraform/providers/ after init.

Q2
What does the version constraint ~> 5.0 mean for a Terraform provider?
Show Answer
Answer

It means ">= 5.0, < 6.0" — any version 5.x.x is allowed, but version 6.0.0 and above are blocked.

Explanation

This is called a "pessimistic constraint." It allows patch and minor updates (5.0.1, 5.1.0, 5.99.0) but blocks major version bumps (6.0.0) that could contain breaking changes. Compare: ~> 5.0 = any 5.x, ~> 5.0.0 = any 5.0.x only, >= 5.0 = any version above 5.0 (dangerous — no upper bound).

Q3
How do you use multiple AWS provider configurations (e.g., for multi-region)?
Show Answer
Answer

Use provider aliases: define provider "aws" { alias = "west"; region = "us-west-2" }, then reference with provider = aws.west in resources.

Explanation
provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" }                    # default
provider "aws" { alias = "west"; region = "us-west-2" }    # aliased
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "dr" { provider = aws.west }      # uses west

Default provider has no alias. Named aliases referenced per resource. Common for DR, multi-region, and cross-account via assume_role.

Q4
What is the difference between implicit and explicit resource dependencies?
Show Answer
Answer

Implicit: Terraform detects dependency from references (e.g., vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id). Explicit: You declare it with depends_on when no reference exists.

Explanation

Implicit dependencies are preferred — they're automatic and always correct. Use depends_on only when there's no actual attribute reference between resources (e.g., a null_resource provisioner that needs an S3 bucket to exist). Overusing depends_on reduces parallelism and slows down applies.

Q5
What does create_before_destroy = true do in a lifecycle block?
Show Answer
Answer

It tells Terraform to create the NEW resource FIRST, verify it's working, and THEN destroy the old resource. This enables zero-downtime updates.

Explanation

This concept is essential for the Terraform Associate exam. Review the related chapter content and practice with `terraform` CLI to reinforce understanding.

Q6
When should you avoid using Terraform provisioners?
Show Answer
Answer

Almost always. Use provider-native features (user_data, cloud-init) or configuration management tools (Ansible) instead. Provisioners are a last resort.

Explanation

Provisioners break Terraform's declarative model: Terraform can't track what the provisioner did, can't revert it, and may not know if it failed. They run only on CREATE (not update). The HashiCorp-recommended pattern is: (1) pre-bake AMIs/Docker images, (2) use user_data/cloud-init for bootstrap, (3) use Ansible/Chef for complex configuration — all invoked OUTSIDE of Terraform provisioners.

Q7
What happens when you change the AMI ID of an aws_instance resource?
Show Answer
Answer

The instance is DESTROYED and RECREATED (shown as -/+ in plan). EC2 does NOT support in-place AMI updates.

Explanation

This concept is essential for the Terraform Associate exam. Review the related chapter content and practice with `terraform` CLI to reinforce understanding.

Q8
How does prevent_destroy = true protect your infrastructure?
Show Answer
Answer

It blocks any attempt to destroy the resource. terraform destroy will ERROR on that resource. You must remove the lifecycle rule before destroying.

Explanation

This concept is essential for the Terraform Associate exam. Review the related chapter content and practice with `terraform` CLI to reinforce understanding.

Q9
What does terraform taint do?
Show Answer
Answer

It marks a resource for destruction and recreation on the next terraform apply. Use when a resource is in a bad state.

$ terraform taint aws_instance.web[0]      # Mark for recreation
$ terraform untaint aws_instance.web[0]    # Remove the mark
$ terraform apply                           # Destroys & recreates web[0]
Explanation

This concept is essential for the Terraform Associate exam. Review the related chapter content and practice with `terraform` CLI to reinforce understanding.

Q10
What are the 4 lifecycle meta-arguments available on every resource?
Show Answer
Answer

1. create_before_destroy — Create new before destroying old. 2. prevent_destroy — Block accidental deletion. 3. ignore_changes — Ignore specific attribute changes. 4. replace_triggered_by — Force recreate when specified attributes change.

Explanation

This concept is essential for the Terraform Associate exam. Review the related chapter content and practice with `terraform` CLI to reinforce understanding.

📋 Part 3 — Implementation Guide & Key Facts

You now understand providers (the bridge to AWS cloud APIs) and resources (the building blocks of AWS infrastructure). Here's how to apply this knowledge in production with anihpj/jobpost on AWS.

🛠️ How to Implement — AWS Provider & Resource Strategy

⚡

AWS Provider & Resource Implementation — 5-Step Production Pattern

1 Step 1: Pin Providers 
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

💡 ~> 5.0 = ">= 5.0, < 6.0" — allows minor/patch updates, blocks breaking 6.x

2 Step 2: Configure Auth 
provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  # Uses: AWS CLI credentials profile
  #   OR: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY env vars
  #   OR: IAM Role (EC2/EKS — best for production)
  #   OR: OIDC Federation (TFC — no static keys!)
}

🔐 NEVER hardcode keys. OIDC = best. IAM Role = great. Env vars = acceptable.

3 Step 3: Write Resources 
resource "aws_vpc" "main" {
  cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16"
}

resource "aws_instance" "web" {
  count         = 3
  ami           = data.aws_ami.ubuntu.id
  instance_type = "t3.micro"
  subnet_id     = aws_subnet.public[count.index].id
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id]
}

🔗 Implicit deps via aws_subnet.public[count.index].id — no depends_on needed!

4 Step 4: Manage Lifecycle 
# Zero-downtime updates (stateless resources)
lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }

# Safety lock (databases, stateful resources)
lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }

# External management (auto-scaling groups)
lifecycle { ignore_changes = [desired_count] }

# Force replace when dependency changes
lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [aws_launch_template.v2.id] }

⚠️ AMI change = DESTROY/RECREATE. Use create_before_destroy for zero downtime!

5 Step 5: Test & Apply — The Quality Gate 
# Quality checks (run before every apply — CI/CD standard)
terraform fmt -check -recursive     # Style check (fails CI if unformatted)
terraform validate                   # Syntax + reference check

# Preview changes (READ ONLY — your safety net)
terraform plan -out=tfplan           # Save plan for exact execution

# Review plan output carefully:
#   Plan: 5 to add, 2 to change, 0 to destroy
#   "Do these changes look right?"

# Apply (after review + approval)
terraform apply tfplan               # Executes exactly what was planned
✅ fmt ✅ validate 🔍 plan 👀 REVIEW 🚀 apply

⚠️ Top 5 Provider/Resource Exam Traps
  1. "terraform import generates .tf code" — FALSE. Import only updates state.
  2. "provisioners are idempotent" — FALSE. They run on CREATE only, not updates.
  3. "count and for_each behave the same" — FALSE. Removing index[1] from count destroys index[2]; for_each keys are stable.
  4. "AMI change = update in-place" — FALSE. AMI change = DESTROY + RECREATE.
  5. "depends_on is always needed" — FALSE. Implicit references handle 99% of dependencies.
✅ Top 5 Provider/Resource Best Practices
  1. Pin ALL provider versions with pessimistic constraints (~> X.Y)
  2. Use for_each over count when resources have meaningful identities
  3. Set prevent_destroy on databases and stateful resources
  4. Use create_before_destroy for zero-downtime deployments
  5. Prefer user_data/cloud-init over provisioners — immutable > mutable
