Part 4: Variables, Outputs & Expressions — From Static to Smart Configs

Hard-coded values are the enemy of reusable infrastructure. In Part 4, you'll learn to make your Terraform configurations dynamic, flexible, and production-ready. Input variables let you parameterize every aspect of your infrastructure — instance sizes, region names, environment labels. Expressions and functions transform data on the fly. Outputs expose critical information to other teams and CI/CD pipelines. Together, these three pillars turn a brittle single-environment config into a multi-environment, multi-region, team-ready infrastructure codebase for anihpj/jobpost.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~4 hours 📖 Ch 9-11 🎯 Domain 4

Chapter 9: Input Variables — Making Configs Flexible & Reusable 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 9: Input Variables — The Foundation of Reusable Infrastructure

Imagine you've written 500 lines of Terraform for anihpj/jobpost in the dev environment. Now you need the same infrastructure in staging and prod. Do you copy-paste and change 37 values? No — you replace those 37 hard-coded values with variables. Input variables are the difference between a one-off script and production-grade infrastructure as code. This chapter covers every aspect: declaration syntax, type system, assignment methods, validation rules, sensitivity, precedence hierarchy, and complex patterns like maps of objects.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 8 Sections 🎯 Domain 4
🎓 TF Associate Relevance
Domain 4: Variables & Outputs ~15% ⚠️ High-Yield

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Declare variables with type, default, description, validation, and sensitive flags
  • ✅ Master all 8 variable types — from simple strings to complex maps of objects
  • ✅ Assign values through 6 different methods — CLI flags, .tfvars files, env vars, defaults
  • ✅ Enforce business rules with custom validation blocks
  • ✅ Protect secrets with sensitive variables and understand their limitations
  • ✅ Memorize the variable precedence hierarchy — the #1 exam topic in Domain 4
  • ✅ Structure complex configs using maps of objects and workspace-based selection
Variable Precedence is THE Most-Tested Topic in Domain 4

If you memorize only one thing from this chapter, make it the variable precedence order. The exam WILL ask you "which value wins?" scenarios. The answer is always: CLI -var > *.auto.tfvars > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_* env vars > default. Every level overrides all levels below it. CLI flags are the nuclear option — they override everything, always.

9.1 Variable Declaration — The Anatomy of a Variable Block

Every input variable in Terraform is declared with a variable block. Think of it as a function parameter for your infrastructure — it says "I need this piece of information, here's what it should look like, and here's what happens if you don't give it to me."

ANATOMY OF A VARIABLE BLOCK — Every Field Explained
  variable "environment" {            ◀── ① NAME: The variable identifier
                                         Used as var.environment in HCL
    type        = string              ◀── ② TYPE: What kind of value?
                                         string, number, bool, list, map,
                                         set, object, tuple, any
    default     = "dev"               ◀── ③ DEFAULT: Fallback value
                                         If omitted, variable is REQUIRED
    description = "Deployment env:    ◀── ④ DESCRIPTION: Human-readable
                   dev, staging,      docs. Shows in terraform plan,
                   or prod"           console, and auto-generated docs
    sensitive   = true                ◀── ⑤ SENSITIVE: Hides from
                                         terraform plan/apply output
                                         ⚠️ Still stored PLAINTEXT in state!
    nullable    = true                ◀── ⑥ NULLABLE: Can value be null?
                                         Default: true (allows null)
    validation {                      ◀── ⑦ VALIDATION: Custom rules
      condition     = contains(       Prevents bad values BEFORE any
        ["dev","staging","prod"],     API call is made
        var.environment)
      error_message = "Must be dev, staging, or prod."
    }
  }
📋 Variable Rules You MUST Know

1. Names must be unique within a module. Two variable "name" blocks = error.

2. No default = required. Terraform will prompt interactively or fail in non-interactive mode.

3. Description shows everywhere. It appears in terraform plan, terraform console, and auto-generated documentation.

4. sensitive only hides output. The value is STILL stored in plaintext in the state file. Use remote state encryption.

5. Variable files are .tfvars or .tfvars.json. Any other extension is ignored unless passed with -var-file.

✅ Best Practices for Variable Declaration

Always add a description. Your future self (and teammates) will thank you. Descriptions are documentation.

Always specify a type. Type constraints catch errors early. type = string is better than no type.

Use sensible defaults. Set defaults for the most common case. Make staging/prod override, not the other way around.

Add validation for enumerated values. If only "dev"/"staging"/"prod" are valid, enforce it with a validation block.

🧠 DEEP DIVE: How Terraform Resolves Variables — The 4-Phase Pipeline
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  Every time you run terraform plan or apply, Terraform executes     ║
  ║  a 4-phase variable resolution pipeline. Understanding this         ║
  ║  pipeline helps you debug "wrong value" issues instantly.           ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  PHASE 1: DECLARATION SCAN (Parse all .tf files)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Terraform scans EVERY .tf file and builds a registry of all         │
  │ declared variables: their names, types, defaults, and constraints.   │
  │                                                                     │
  │ If two variable blocks have the same name → IMMEDIATE ERROR.        │
  │ If a variable block has no type → type defaults to "any" (⚠️ loose).│
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
  PHASE 2: VALUE COLLECTION (Gather values from all 6 sources)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Terraform collects values in a specific ORDER (lowest priority      │
  │ first, highest priority last — so higher values overwrite lower):   │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ① Read variable defaults from variable blocks                      │
  │  ② Read TF_VAR_* environment variables                              │
  │  ③ Read terraform.tfvars (if exists)                                │
  │  ④ Read terraform.tfvars.json (if exists)                           │
  │  ⑤ Read *.auto.tfvars and *.auto.tfvars.json (alphabetical order)   │
  │  ⑥ Apply CLI -var and -var-file flags (LAST one wins)               │
  │                                                                     │
  │ EACH step OVERWRITES values from previous steps. The value at       │
  │ step ⑥ is the FINAL value — nothing can override it.                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
  PHASE 3: TYPE CHECKING & COERCION (Validate and convert)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Terraform checks the collected value against the declared type:     │
  │                                                                     │
  │ ✅ string "8000" can be coerced to number 8000 (automatic)          │
  │ ✅ number 8000 can be coerced to string "8000" (automatic)          │
  │ ✅ string "true" can be coerced to bool true (automatic)            │
  │ ❌ string "hello" can NOT be coerced to number → TYPE ERROR         │
  │ ❌ number 42 can NOT be coerced to list(string) → TYPE ERROR        │
  │                                                                     │
  │ Single values are auto-wrapped in lists: "a" → ["a"]                │
  │ Strings are auto-converted to numbers when the target is number.    │
  │ BUT: booleans are STRICT. "true" (string) ≠ true (bool).            │
  │                                                                     │
  │ ⚠️  KEY INSIGHT: Terraform is LENIENT with string↔number, but      │
  │     STRICT with booleans. This leniency hides bugs — always use     │
  │     explicit types to avoid surprises.                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
                                    ▼
  PHASE 4: VALIDATION EXECUTION (Run custom rules)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Every validation{} block in the variable declaration is executed:   │
  │                                                                     │
  │ • All validations run IN PARALLEL — order doesn't matter            │
  │ • If ANY validation fails → terraform plan/apply STOPS immediately  │
  │ • error_message is displayed to the user                            │
  │ • NO API calls have been made yet (pure configuration check)        │
  │                                                                     │
  │ 💡 This is why validations are SO valuable: they catch              │
  │    misconfigurations before a single cloud resource is touched.     │
  │    You can have 20 validation blocks on one variable — each         │
  │    independently checks a different rule.                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  POST-RESOLUTION: The final value is now available as var.environment
  everywhere in your HCL code. Any reference to var. reads
  this resolved value.
🧠 Why Understanding This Pipeline Matters

Debugging "wrong value" issues: If your variable has an unexpected value, trace it through the pipeline. Which source is winning? Is a higher-priority source overriding your intended value?

CI/CD troubleshooting: In CI/CD, TF_VAR_* env vars are common. If your CI pipeline sets TF_VAR_environment=staging but your terraform.tfvars also sets environment = "dev", the env var WINS (higher priority). This can cause confusion if you're not aware of the pipeline.

Testing variable resolution: Use terraform console to test: var.environment shows the resolved value. terraform plan also shows variable values in the output (unless sensitive).

9.2 Variable Types — From Simple Strings to Complex Objects

Terraform's type system is one of its most powerful features. Choosing the right type prevents entire categories of bugs at plan time — before any API call is made. Let's explore every type with real anihpj/jobpost examples.

🧠 Type Conversion: What Terraform Accepts

Terraform automatically converts types when possible: "8000" can become 8000 if the target is number. A single value becomes a list automatically: "us-east-1a" → ["us-east-1a"]. But "true" does NOT become true — booleans are strict. Exam tip: if you see "true" assigned to a bool variable, that's a type error.

🧬 DEEP DIVE: Type Coercion & Conversion — ALL the Rules

Terraform's type coercion is "lenient but principled." It tries to make your value fit the declared type — but only when the conversion is unambiguous.

RULE 1
Automatic String ↔ Number Conversion

Terraform freely converts between strings and numbers when the target type is clear. This is the most forgiving coercion rule — it exists because many cloud provider APIs return numbers as strings (e.g., port numbers from AWS API responses, or .tfvars files where port = 8000 is parsed as a number). Terraform bridges the gap so you don't have to think about it. But this leniency has a limit: the string must be purely numeric. "8000" converts cleanly. "hello" crashes. And booleans never auto-convert to strings — that's a separate rule entirely.

✅ "8000" → 8000 (numeric string to number)
✅ 8000 → "8000" (number to string representation)
❌ "hello" → number (non-numeric string → TYPE ERROR)
❌ true → "true" (booleans do NOT auto-coerce to strings)
RULE 2
Bool Is Strict — NO Implicit Conversions

Booleans are completely isolated from the rest of the type system. Unlike string/number which freely interconvert, true/false only match bool — nothing else. This is the #1 type error beginners make because most programming languages are looser with booleans. Python accepts 1 == True. JavaScript coerces "true" in conditionals. Terraform does none of that. This strictness is intentional: infrastructure decisions (enable_monitoring, multi_az, deletion_protection) are binary and consequential. A silent coercion from "false" (string) to false (bool) could disable production safeguards. Terraform forces you to be explicit.

✅ true, false → bool (unquoted, lowercase ONLY)
❌ "true", "false" → bool (quoted strings — still strings!)
❌ "TRUE", "FALSE" → bool (uppercase — never valid)
❌ 1, 0 → bool (numbers — will NOT become true/false)

⚠️ #1 Type-Related Exam Trap. The exam will show you "true" (with quotes) assigned to a bool variable and ask "Will this work?" The answer is NO. Always use unquoted true/false, always lowercase.

RULE 3
Singletons Auto-Wrap into Lists

When a variable is typed as list(<T>) but you provide a single value of type T, Terraform automatically wraps it: "a" becomes ["a"]. This is a convenience feature — most of the time you have one value, but the variable type says "this could be a list." Without auto-wrap, you'd write redundant brackets everywhere: var.azs = ["us-east-1a"] instead of var.azs = "us-east-1a". However, this convenience can mask bugs: if you forget to provide a list when you actually meant to, Terraform silently wraps a single value and creates one resource instead of three. No error, just wrong behavior. For critical multi-resource variables, always use explicit brackets to make intent visible.

✅ "a" → list(string) = ["a"] (one-element list)
✅ 8000 → list(number) = [8000] (one-element list)
✅ true → list(bool) = [true] (one-element list)

💡 Real-world example: variable "azs" { type = list(string); default = "us-east-1a" } works fine — Terraform wraps it into ["us-east-1a"]. But if a teammate meant to write ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b"] and forgot the brackets, you get one AZ instead of two — silently.

RULE 4
Maps & Lists — Structural Type Checking

Once you declare a type like list(string) or map(number), Terraform enforces it deeply — every single element must match the inner type. This is fundamentally different from the "lenient" string/number conversion. If list(string) contains one number, the WHOLE configuration fails at plan time. This strictness is critical for infrastructure code: a list of subnet CIDRs is meaningless if one entry is an integer. A map of instance sizes is worthless if one value is a list. Terraform refuses to guess — it fails loudly so you fix the data at the source rather than deploying broken infrastructure. This is the rule that catches the most subtle .tfvars bugs.

✅ ["a","b"] → list(string) (all strings)
✅ {key = "val"} → map(string) (all values strings)
❌ ["a", 1] → list(string) (index 1 is a number, not string)
❌ {a = 1, b = "2"} → map(number) (b is string, not number)

Structural types (list, map, set, object, tuple) require EXACT type matches for every element. No leniency, no auto-conversion within collections.

RULE 5
Object/Tuple — Named Field Matching

Objects are Terraform's strictest type constraint. When you declare an object with specific fields, Terraform requires an exact match: every named field must be present, with the correct type, and no extra fields are allowed. This is by design — objects represent structured configuration units where every field has semantic meaning. A missing port on a service config means the service can't run. An extra typo'd field like portt = 80 would be silently ignored if Terraform allowed extras, leading to "why is my port 8080 not 80?" debugging nightmares. Terraform catches these at plan time — before a single API call. For anihpj/jobpost, this means the jobpost_config object must match exactly, preventing Docker/K8s/database misconfigurations.

object({name: string, port: number}) requires exactly those fields:
✅ {name = "web", port = 80} (exact match — both fields present)
❌ {name = "web"} (missing required field: port)
❌ {name = "web", port = 80, host = "x"} (extra field: host not declared)

Think of objects as a contract: you define the exact shape, and Terraform enforces it. No missing fields, no surprise extras. This is what makes complex variables safe at scale.

RULE 6
any Type — The Wildcard (Avoid in Production!)

type = any is Terraform's escape hatch. It accepts anything: strings, numbers, booleans, lists, maps, objects, null — no questions asked. It exists for three specific reasons: (1) quick prototyping when the final type isn't decided yet, (2) migrating legacy configurations where types are uncertain, and (3) rare cases where a variable genuinely needs to accept multiple unrelated types. In all other scenarios, any is a liability. It disables Terraform's type-checking safety net. It provides zero documentation — a teammate reading your code has no idea what values are valid. It silently accepts wrong types that would otherwise be caught at plan time. The exam knows this is controversial and will test your judgment: "any is valid" (TRUE), but "any is recommended" (FALSE — use explicit types).

✅ Accepts: string | number | bool | list | map | object | null
❌ No validation, no type safety, no self-documentation.

Exam trap: "any is a valid Terraform type" → TRUE. "any is recommended for production configurations" → FALSE. Valid only for prototyping and migration. In production, always use a specific type.

💡 Quick Recall — The 6 Coercion Rules at a Glance

1. String ↔ Number auto-converts freely (both directions) | 2. Bools are completely isolated — no coercion from any type | 3. Singletons auto-wrap: "x" becomes ["x"] for list-typed variables | 4. Structural types need exact inner-type matches for every element | 5. Objects require all declared fields, no extras allowed | 6. any bypasses all checking — use only when you must.

anihpj/jobpost: Complex Variable for Docker + K8s Config
variable "jobpost_config" {
  description = "Complete configuration for jobpost Django application"
  type = object({
    docker = object({
      image_tag    = string
      registry_url = string
    })
    kubernetes = object({
      replicas        = number
      cpu_request     = string
      memory_request  = string
      cpu_limit       = string
      memory_limit    = string
    })
    database = object({
      engine         = string
      version        = string
      instance_class = string
      storage_gb     = number
      backup_retention_days = number
    })
  })
  default = {
    docker = {
      image_tag    = "latest"
      registry_url = "123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com"
    }
    kubernetes = {
      replicas       = 3
      cpu_request    = "250m"
      memory_request = "256Mi"
      cpu_limit      = "500m"
      memory_limit   = "512Mi"
    }
    database = {
      engine         = "postgres"
      version        = "16.1"
      instance_class = "db.t3.medium"
      storage_gb     = 20
      backup_retention_days = 7
    }
  }
}

# Usage in resources:
resource "kubernetes_deployment" "jobpost" {
  spec {
    replicas = var.jobpost_config.kubernetes.replicas
    template {
      spec {
        container {
          image = "${var.jobpost_config.docker.registry_url}:${var.jobpost_config.docker.image_tag}"
          resources {
            requests = {
              cpu    = var.jobpost_config.kubernetes.cpu_request
              memory = var.jobpost_config.kubernetes.memory_request
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

9.3 Variable Assignment Methods — 6 Ways to Feed Values In

Terraform gives you six different ways to assign values to variables. Each has a specific priority level and use case. Understanding when to use each method is critical for both the exam and real-world CI/CD pipelines.

THE 6 VARIABLE ASSIGNMENT METHODS — Priority from Highest to Lowest
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              VARIABLE ASSIGNMENT PRECEDENCE HIERARCHY               │
  │              (🥇 = highest priority, overrides everything below)    │
  │                                                                     │
  │  🥇 METHOD 1: CLI -var FLAG                                        │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ terraform apply -var="environment=prod"                     │ │
  │  │ $ terraform apply -var='ports=[80,443]'                       │ │

  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              ▲                                      │
  │  🥇 METHOD 2: CLI -var-file FLAG                                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ terraform apply -var-file="prod.tfvars"                     │ │
  │  │ Same priority as -var. If both set, last one wins.            │ │
  │  │ Use for: CI/CD pipelines, one-off manual deployments.         │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              ▲                                      │

  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ ls *.auto.tfvars                                            │ │
  │  │ production.auto.tfvars   staging.auto.tfvars                  │ │
  │  │ AUTO-LOADED — no flag needed. Any file matching *.auto.tfvars │ │
  │  │ ⚠️  EXAM GOTCHA: *.auto.tfvars BEATS terraform.tfvars!       │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              ▲                                      │
  │  🥉 METHOD 4: terraform.tfvars / terraform.tfvars.json             │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ $ cat terraform.tfvars                                        │ │

  │  │ Use for: Shared team defaults, checked into Git.              │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              ▲                                      │

9.4 Variable Validation — Gatekeeping Values Before They Break Things

Custom validation rules are Terraform's built-in guardrails. They check variable values before any API call is made, catching configuration errors at plan time instead of 20 minutes into an apply. Every validation block has a condition (must evaluate to true) and an error_message (shown when it fails).

CUSTOM VALIDATION — 5 Production-Ready Examples for anihpj/jobpost
PATTERN 1
Enumerated Values — Allow-List Strings

The most common validation pattern. You have a fixed set of valid values (environments, regions, instance sizes) and want to reject everything else. contains(list, value) checks if the value is in the list — it's simple, fast, and the error message tells users exactly what's allowed. This catches typos like "production" when only "prod" is valid, or "us-est-1" instead of "us-east-1". Every enumerated variable should have this validation.

HCL
variable "environment" {
  type = string
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev","staging","prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "Environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

$ terraform plan -var="environment=production"
╔══════════════════════════════════════╗
║ Error: Invalid value for variable ║
║ Environment must be dev, staging, ║
║ or prod. ║
╚══════════════════════════════════════╝

PATTERN 2
Length Constraints — String & Number Bounds

Cloud providers impose hard limits on resource names. AWS RDS database names must be 1-63 characters. S3 bucket names must be 3-63 characters. IAM role names: 1-64. Rather than letting Terraform fail 15 minutes into an apply with a cryptic AWS error, catch the violation at plan time with a clear message. The length() function works on strings, lists, and maps — this pattern applies to all three. For the anihpj/jobpost database, this prevents deploying with an invalid name that AWS would reject.

HCL
variable "db_name" {
  type = string
  validation {
    condition     = length(var.db_name) >= 3 &&
                    length(var.db_name) <= 63
    error_message = "DB name must be 3-63 characters."
  }
}

💡 Combine with can(regex(...)) to also enforce valid characters (only lowercase, numbers, hyphens for most cloud resources).

PATTERN 3
Regex Patterns — Validate Format

When simple allow-lists aren't enough, regular expressions handle structural validation: domain names, IP addresses, email formats, Kubernetes resource names, and any pattern-based rule. The critical technique here is wrapping regex() in can(). Without can(), a non-matching regex throws an unhandled error that crashes the entire plan — not just the validation. With can(), a non-match returns false cleanly, and validation fails with your custom error_message. Never use raw regex() in a validation condition.

HCL
variable "domain_name" {
  type = string
  validation {
    condition     = can(regex(
      "^[a-z0-9.-]+\\.[a-z]{2,}$",
      var.domain_name
    ))
    error_message = "Domain must be a valid FQDN (e.g., anihpj.com)."
  }
}

⚠️ Exam trap: The exam WILL show you a validation block using raw regex() without can() and ask "What happens when the pattern doesn't match?" Answer: The plan crashes with an error, not a clean validation failure. Always use can(regex(...)).

PATTERN 4
Numeric Ranges — Min/Max Value Gates

Numbers need guardrails too. Kubernetes replicas below 0? Nonsensical. RDS storage below 20GB with backups enabled? AWS will reject it. Auto-scaling group sizes beyond account limits? Apply will fail mid-way. Numeric range validations catch these before any cloud API call. The pattern is always var.<name> >= min && var.<name> <= max. For the anihpj/jobpost Kubernetes deployment, this ensures nobody accidentally sets replicas to 0 (taking the app down) or 100 (exceeding node capacity or budget). The limits should match your actual infrastructure constraints — don't just copy these numbers.

HCL
variable "k8s_replicas" {
  type = number
  validation {
    condition     = var.k8s_replicas >= 1 &&
                    var.k8s_replicas <= 10
    error_message = "K8s replicas must be between 1 and 10."
  }
}
PATTERN 5
Cross-Field Validation — One Field Depends on Another

The most powerful validation pattern — and the hardest to get right. When one variable field's validity depends on another, you need a cross-field check. In this example: if backups are enabled (backup_retention > 0), then storage must be at least 20GB (AWS RDS minimum for backups). If backups are disabled, any storage size is fine. The conditional expression condition ? check : true means "only enforce the check when the condition is true — otherwise pass." This pattern scales to any interdependent fields: "if Multi-AZ is enabled, instance class must be at least db.t3.small," or "if environment is prod, deletion_protection must be true." These cross-field rules prevent entire categories of production misconfigurations.

HCL
variable "storage_config" {
  type = object({
    storage_gb       = number
    backup_retention = number
  })
  validation {
    condition     = var.storage_config.backup_retention > 0 ?
                    var.storage_config.storage_gb >= 20 : true
    error_message = "Backups require at least 20GB storage."
  }
}

💡 Pattern formula: condition ? (var.field_1 >= constraint) : true — "If the triggering condition is met, enforce the constraint. Otherwise, let anything through." This makes validations conditional instead of always-on.

🧠 Validation Rules — What the Exam Tests

1. condition must evaluate to bool. If it returns a string or number, it's a type error.

2. Multiple validations are allowed. One variable can have many validation{} blocks — each is checked independently.

3. Validation runs at plan time. This means NO API calls, NO cost, NO risk. Pure syntax/semantic check.

4. error_message is required. If you forget it, Terraform won't even parse the file.

5. can() is your friend. Wrap regex or other functions in can() to gracefully handle errors instead of crashing.

9.5 Sensitive Variables — Protecting Secrets in Terraform

Setting sensitive = true on a variable hides its value from console output during terraform plan and terraform apply. But here's the critical exam fact: sensitive does NOT encrypt the value in state. The value is still stored as plaintext in terraform.tfstate. You need defense in depth.

THE SENSITIVE VARIABLE LIFECYCLE — Where Secrets Travel
  variable "db_password" {
    type      = string
    sensitive = true
    description = "RDS master password"
  }

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    🔐 SECRET FLOW THROUGH TERRAFORM              │
  │                                                                  │
  │  🔐 SOURCE                    📍 INTERMEDIATE                     │
  │  ┌──────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐            │
  │  │ Vault / AWS  │───fetch───▶│ TF_VAR_db_password   │            │
  │  │ Secrets Mgr  │            │ (env var in CI/CD)    │            │
  │  │ / SSM Param  │            └──────────┬───────────┘            │
  │  └──────────────┘                       │                        │
  │                                         ▼                        │
  │  🔒 CONSOLE OUTPUT                ⚠️  STATE FILE                 │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐            ┌──────────────────────┐       │
  │  │ terraform plan   │            │ terraform.tfstate    │       │
  │  │   + db_password  │            │ "db_password":       │       │
  │  │     = (sensitive │◀───────────│  "correcthorsebat..." │       │
  │  │       value)     │            │ ⚠️  PLAIN TEXT!       │       │
  │  │ ✅ REDACTED      │            └──────────────────────┘       │
  │  └──────────────────┘                                           │
  │                                                                  │
  │  🛡️ PROTECTION STACK (defense in depth):                        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ 1. sensitive = true       → Hides from console output      │ │
  │  │ 2. Remote state encryption → S3 SSE-KMS / Azure Storage    │ │
  │  │ 3. TF_VAR_* in CI/CD      → GitHub Secrets / GitLab CI var │ │
  │  │ 4. Vault dynamic secrets  → Auto-rotate, short-lived TTL  │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ What sensitive = true does NOT do

❌ Does NOT encrypt the state file

❌ Does NOT prevent the value from being stored in state

❌ Does NOT encrypt values in transit

❌ Does NOT prevent the value from appearing in error messages (sometimes)

❌ Does NOT encrypt .tfvars files

✅ What sensitive = true DOES do

✅ Hides value from terraform plan output

✅ Hides value from terraform apply output

✅ Hides value from terraform output (if output is also sensitive)

✅ Prevents the value from appearing in logs

✅ Marks the variable as sensitive in auto-generated docs

⚠️ EXAM HOTSPOT: sensitive does NOT encrypt state

This is one of the most common trick questions on the exam. They'll say "setting sensitive=true encrypts the variable in the state file" — this is FALSE. The state file stores ALL values in plaintext regardless of sensitivity. You must use remote state with encryption (S3 SSE-KMS, Azure Storage encryption) to protect state at rest. sensitive=true only controls what's displayed to humans, not what's stored.

9.6 Variable Definition Precedence — Who Wins When Values Conflict?

When the same variable is set in multiple places, Terraform uses a strict priority system to resolve the conflict. This is the single most-tested topic in Domain 4. Memorize this hierarchy cold.

VARIABLE PRECEDENCE HIERARCHY — The Definitive Diagram (Memorize This!)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                      │
  │     🥇 LEVEL 1: CLI -var / -var-file                                 │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │     │ $ terraform apply -var="env=prod"                          │  │
  │     │ ☢️  NUCLEAR OPTION — Overrides EVERYTHING below            │  │
  │     │ If both -var and -var-file set, the LAST one wins          │  │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                       │
  │                              ▼ OVERRIDES                             │
  │     🥈 LEVEL 2: *.auto.tfvars & *.auto.tfvars.json                  │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │     │ $ cat staging.auto.tfvars                                  │  │
  │     │ environment = "staging"                                    │  │
  │     │ ✅ Auto-loaded — no flag needed                            │  │
  │     │ ✅ Multiple *.auto.tfvars files are all loaded (alphabet.)  │  │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                       │
  │                              ▼ OVERRIDES                             │
  │     🥉 LEVEL 3: terraform.tfvars & terraform.tfvars.json            │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │     │ $ cat terraform.tfvars                                     │  │
  │     │ environment = "development"                                │  │
  │     │ ✅ Auto-loaded if file exists                              │  │
  │     │ ⚠️  GETS OVERRIDDEN by *.auto.tfvars!                     │  │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                       │
  │                              ▼ OVERRIDES                             │
  │     LEVEL 4: TF_VAR_* Environment Variables                         │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │     │ $ export TF_VAR_environment=staging                        │  │
  │     │ $ export TF_VAR_db_password=secret123                      │  │
  │     │ ⚠️  NOT auto-loaded files — read from shell env            │  │
  │     │ ⚠️  Prefix TF_VAR_ is CASE-SENSITIVE                      │  │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                              │                                       │
  │                              ▼ OVERRIDES                             │
  │     LEVEL 5: Variable Default Value                                  │
  │     ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │     │ variable "environment" { default = "dev" }                 │  │
  │     │ 📌 Last resort — only used if NOTHING else provides value  │  │
  │     └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  │                                                                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 EXAM MNEMONIC: "Cats Always Try Fish"

CLI -var → Auto.tfvars → Terraform.tfvars → F_VAR_* env → Default. Or remember: "Command line Always Takes First place" — the CLI is always the highest priority. Every lower level only applies if no higher level has set the variable.

🧪 DEEP DIVE: Real-World Precedence Conflict — 6 Sources, One Winner
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  SCENARIO: You have 6 different sources ALL trying to set the       ║
  ║  variable "environment" for anihpj/jobpost. Which one wins?         ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  DECLARATION (variables.tf):
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ variable "environment" { type = string; default = "dev" }            │
  │                              └─────── source ⑥ (lowest) ──────┘     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  SOURCE ⑥: Default Value           → "dev"        ← Fallback only
  SOURCE ⑤: TF_VAR_environment      → "staging"    ← Shell: export TF_VAR_environment=staging
  SOURCE ④: terraform.tfvars        → "production" ← File: environment = "production"
  SOURCE ③: staging.auto.tfvars     → "staging"    ← File: environment = "staging"
  SOURCE ②: prod.auto.tfvars        → "prod"       ← File: environment = "prod"
  SOURCE ①: CLI -var                → "emergency"  ← Flag: -var="environment=emergency"

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  RESOLUTION (highest priority wins):
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  Step 1: Start with default      → environment = "dev"
  Step 2: TF_VAR_ overrides       → environment = "staging"  (⑤ beats ⑥)
  Step 3: terraform.tfvars overrides → environment = "production" (④ beats ⑤)
  Step 4: staging.auto.tfvars overrides → environment = "staging" (③ beats ④)
  Step 5: prod.auto.tfvars overrides → environment = "prod" (② beats ③)
  Step 6: CLI -var overrides       → environment = "emergency" (① beats ALL)

  🏆 FINAL RESULT: var.environment = "emergency"   ← CLI ALWAYS wins

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  KEY INSIGHTS FROM THIS SCENARIO:
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  1. Each source OVERWRITES the previous — it's NOT a merge.
     The final value is from the single highest-priority source.

  2. Multiple *.auto.tfvars files are loaded in ALPHABETICAL order.
     prod.auto.tfvars (p) loads AFTER staging.auto.tfvars (s).
     So prod.auto.tfvars WINS between the two.

  3. CLI -var is the "break glass in emergency" option.
     If everything else is misconfigured, -var saves you.

  4. The default value is only used if NO OTHER source sets it.
     In this scenario, "dev" never makes it past step 1.

  5. ⚠️  If you DON'T use CLI -var, then prod.auto.tfvars (②) wins.
     The final value would be "prod", NOT "staging" or "production".
     Many teams are surprised by this!
🔴 Common Precedence Surprises

"I set TF_VAR_* but it's not working!" → Check if terraform.tfvars or *.auto.tfvars exists. Those OVERRIDE env vars.

"My *.auto.tfvars is being ignored!" → Check the filename. Must match *.auto.tfvars pattern. config.tfvars is NOT auto-loaded.

"Why is staging winning over prod?" → *.auto.tfvars loads in alphabetical order. staging.auto.tfvars (s) comes before prod.auto.tfvars — wait, prod comes AFTER staging alphabetically? No: 'p' > 's'. So prod.auto.tfvars actually wins! But if you have dev.auto.tfvars, it loads first and gets overridden.

🟢 Best Practices for Avoiding Conflicts

1. Use ONE *.auto.tfvars per environment. Don't mix dev/staging/prod in the same directory.

2. Put environment-specific values in .tfvars, NOT in variable defaults. Defaults should be the "safest" value (dev), not production values.

3. In CI/CD, pass sensitive values via TF_VAR_* env vars. Use GitHub Secrets → TF_VAR_* for passwords and keys.

4. Never use -var in production pipelines. It hides values from your codebase. Reserve -var for emergency manual interventions only.

5. Document which sources are active in your team's README. "Variables come from prod.auto.tfvars + TF_VAR_db_password from CI secrets."

9.7 Complex Variable Patterns — Maps of Objects & Lists of Maps

As your infrastructure grows, simple variables aren't enough. You need structured data — maps of objects that define entire environment configurations in one variable. This is the pattern used by every production Terraform codebase.

COMPLEX VARIABLE PATTERN — Maps of Objects for anihpj/jobpost
  variable "environments" {
    description = "Per-environment configuration for anihpj/jobpost"
    type = map(object({
      instance_type   = string
      min_size        = number
      max_size        = number
      enable_monitoring = bool
      k8s_namespace   = string
      db_instance     = string
      db_storage      = number
    }))
    default = {
      dev = {
        instance_type     = "t3.micro"
        min_size          = 1
        max_size          = 2
        enable_monitoring = false
        k8s_namespace     = "anihpj-dev"
        db_instance       = "db.t3.micro"
        db_storage        = 20
      }
      staging = {
        instance_type     = "t3.small"
        min_size          = 2
        max_size          = 4
        enable_monitoring = true
        k8s_namespace     = "anihpj-staging"
        db_instance       = "db.t3.small"
        db_storage        = 50
      }
      prod = {
        instance_type     = "t3.medium"
        min_size          = 3
        max_size          = 10
        enable_monitoring = true
        k8s_namespace     = "anihpj-prod"
        db_instance       = "db.t3.medium"
        db_storage        = 100
      }
    }
  }

  # USAGE: ONE resource block, ALL environments — iterate with for_each
  resource "kubernetes_namespace" "anihpj" {
    for_each = var.environments
    metadata { name = each.value.k8s_namespace }
  }

  # Access specific env: var.environments["prod"].db_storage → 100
🗺️ Map of Objects

Best for: Environment-specific configs. Each key (dev/staging/prod) maps to a complete object.

Access: var.config["dev"].size

Iterate with: for_each

📋 List of Objects

Best for: Ordered collections. Each item is a complete object at a numeric index.

Access: var.config[0].size

Iterate with: count

🧩 List of Maps

Best for: Simpler ordered collections where objects aren't needed.

Access: var.config[0]["key"]

Iterate with: count or for

9.8 Environment-Specific Variables — Workspace-Based Selection

Terraform workspaces let you use the same code to deploy to different environments. The terraform.workspace variable tells you which workspace is active, and you can use it with lookup() or try() to select environment-specific values.

Workspace-Based Environment Selection for anihpj/jobpost
variable "instance_config" {
  type = map(object({
    size  = string
    count = number
  }))
  default = {
    dev     = { size = "t3.micro",  count = 1 }
    staging = { size = "t3.small",  count = 2 }
    prod    = { size = "t3.medium", count = 3 }
  }
}

locals {
  config = lookup(var.instance_config, terraform.workspace,
                   var.instance_config["dev"])  # dev is fallback
}

resource "aws_instance" "anihpj" {
  count         = local.config.count
  instance_type = local.config.size
  tags = {
    Name        = "anihpj-${terraform.workspace}"
    Environment = terraform.workspace
  }
}

# $ terraform workspace select dev    → 1× t3.micro
# $ terraform workspace select prod   → 3× t3.medium
# SAME code → DIFFERENT infrastructure!
🧠 terraform.workspace — Key Facts

Default workspace = "default". Always exists, can't be deleted.

Available everywhere in HCL. Use it in locals, resources, outputs — anywhere.

Not suitable for strong isolation. Workspaces share the same backend and credentials. For hard isolation, use separate backends (different S3 buckets) or separate directories.

Works with Terraform Cloud workspaces too. TFC workspaces map to CLI workspaces seamlessly.

📝 Chapter 9 — Terraform Associate Practice Questions

Q1
What is the HIGHEST priority method for setting a variable value in Terraform?
Show Answer
Answer

CLI -var and -var-file flags (tied for highest priority).

Explanation

The CLI flags -var and -var-file override ALL other variable assignment methods. The full precedence order (highest to lowest) is:

CLI -var/-var-file → *.auto.tfvars → terraform.tfvars → TF_VAR_* env vars → default

Between -var and -var-file, if both are used for the same variable, the one specified LAST wins.

Q2
You set sensitive = true on a variable. Which of the following is TRUE?
Show Answer
Answer

The value is hidden from terraform plan and terraform apply console output, but is still stored in plaintext in the state file.

# Example usage:
terraform plan -out=tfplan

sensitive = true only controls what's displayed — it does NOT encrypt the state file. To protect secrets at rest:

1. Use remote state with encryption (S3 + SSE-KMS)
2. Store secrets in Vault / AWS Secrets Manager
3. Use TF_VAR_* env vars from CI/CD secret stores
4. NEVER commit .tfvars with secrets to Git
Q3
You have terraform.tfvars AND production.auto.tfvars in the same directory. Both set environment. Which value wins?
Show Answer
Answer

production.auto.tfvars wins because *.auto.tfvars has HIGHER priority than terraform.tfvars.

Explanation

This is one of the most commonly tested precedence scenarios:

*.auto.tfvars  (LEVEL 2) — AUTO-LOADED, HIGHER PRIORITY
      │
      ▼ OVERRIDES
terraform.tfvars (LEVEL 3) — AUTO-LOADED, LOWER PRIORITY

Both files are auto-loaded, but *.auto.tfvars always beats
terraform.tfvars when there's a conflict.
Q4
Which variable type would you use to ensure each value is unique and order doesn't matter?
Show Answer
Answer

set(<type>) — an unordered collection of unique values.

Explanation
TypeOrdered?Unique?Access
list✅❌index [0]
set❌✅for_each only
map❌✅ (keys)key ["name"]

Use set(string) for allowed ports or availability zones where duplicates are meaningless.

Q5
A variable has NO default value and NO value is provided through any method. What happens when you run terraform plan?
Show Answer
Answer

Terraform prompts interactively for the value. In non-interactive mode (CI/CD), it fails with an error.

terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
n

Variables without defaults are required inputs:

INTERACTIVE TERMINAL:  Prompts user: "var.name: Enter a value"
NON-INTERACTIVE (CI):  Error: No value for required variable

SOLUTION: Always provide a default OR pass via -var,
-var-file, *.auto.tfvars, terraform.tfvars, or TF_VAR_* env var.
Q6
You need a variable that accepts either a string, a number, or a list. Which type should you use?
Show Answer
Answer

any — accepts any type. Use sparingly as it defeats type safety.

Explanation

type = any is flexible but dangerous. The exam may ask: "any" is a valid type → TRUE. But best practice is to use specific types.

Q7
What is the purpose of the validation block inside a variable block?
Show Answer
Answer

To enforce custom rules on variable values BEFORE any infrastructure API call is made. Validation runs at plan time.

Explanation
variable "environment" {
  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev","staging","prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "Environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

$ terraform plan -var="environment=production"
╔═══════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║ Error: Invalid value for variable            ║
║ Environment must be dev, staging, or prod.   ║
╚═══════════════════════════════════════════════╝
✅ Caught BEFORE any AWS API call!
Q8
How do you reference an environment variable named TF_VAR_region inside your HCL code?
Show Answer
Answer

As var.region. Terraform strips the TF_VAR_ prefix and maps env vars to variables automatically.

Explanation
# Shell: export TF_VAR_region=us-east-1
# HCL:  variable "region" { type = string }
# Usage: var.region  → "us-east-1" (NOT "TF_VAR_region")
Q9
Which variable file names will be auto-loaded by Terraform? (Select TWO)
Show Answer
Answer

terraform.tfvars and staging.auto.tfvars are auto-loaded. custom.tfvars and vars.tf are NOT.

Explanation
✅ terraform.tfvars         ✅ *.auto.tfvars
✅ terraform.tfvars.json    ✅ *.auto.tfvars.json
❌ custom.tfvars (needs -var-file flag)
❌ vars.tf (config file, not variable file)
Q10
You have a variable of type object({name: string, ports: list(number)}). How do you access the second port?
Show Answer
Answer

var.config.ports[1] — dot notation for object fields, bracket notation for list index (0-based).

Explanation
var.config.name      → "anihpj"     (dot notation)
var.config.ports[0]  → 80           (bracket, 0-based)
var.config.ports[1]  → 443          (second element)

🔑 Ch9 Key Takeaways — Input Variables Mastered

📥Variable Precedence

CLI -var > *.auto.tfvars > terraform.tfvars > TF_VAR_env > default. Memorize this order — it's tested on every exam.

🔒Sensitive Variables

sensitive = true hides value in plan/apply output. Does NOT encrypt in state. Use Vault/Secrets Manager for true secret protection.

✅Validation Blocks

validation { condition = ... error_message = ... } — catch bad inputs early. Use can(regex(...)) for safe pattern matching.

📦Type Constraints

string, number, bool, list(type), map(type), object({...}), tuple([...]), any. Complex types = safer configs.

🗺️Maps for Environments

One map(object) variable → all environments. Replace 100 lines of per-env config with one data structure. The clean way to scale.

🏗️Struct Patterns

.tfvars files per workspace. Variable sets in TFC for shared config. Never commit .tfvars with secrets. Separate data from code.

Chapter 10: Expressions, Functions & Conditionals 🟡 Intermediate

Chapter 10: Expressions, Functions & Conditionals — HCL's Power Tools

Variables store data. Expressions and functions transform it. This is where HCL stops being a configuration format and starts being a programming language. You'll learn to use conditional logic (? :), list/map transformations (for expressions), wildcard operations ([*] splat), 100+ built-in functions, dynamic blocks, and error handling — all to make your infrastructure code smarter, shorter, and more maintainable for anihpj/jobpost.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~1.5 hours 📖 10 Sections 🎯 Domain 4
🎓 TF Associate Relevance
Domain 4: Variables & Outputs ~15%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Master string interpolation — "${var.name}" and template directives %{if}
  • ✅ Use arithmetic (+ - * / %) and logical (&& || !) operators
  • ✅ Write conditional expressions — condition ? true_val : false_val
  • ✅ Transform lists and maps with for expressions — filtering, mapping, grouping
  • ✅ Apply splat expressions [*] to extract attributes from resource lists

10.1 String Interpolation — "${var.name}" and Template Syntax

String interpolation embeds variable values directly into strings. The syntax "${...}" evaluates any expression and converts the result to a string. For multi-line templates with conditionals and loops, use the template directive syntax %{...}.

STRING INTERPOLATION — All 4 Patterns with Examples
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 1: Simple interpolation                                    ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  "Hello, ${var.username}"               → "Hello, admin"            ║
  ║  "ami-${var.ami_id}"                    → "ami-0a1b2c3d"            ║
  ║  "${var.region}-${var.environment}"      → "us-east-1-prod"          ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 2: Template directives (%{...}) — Multi-line with logic    ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  user_data = <<-EOT                                                   ║
  ║  #!/bin/bash                                                         ║
  ║  echo "Deploying anihpj ${var.version}"                              ║
  ║  %{ if var.environment == "prod" }                                   ║
  ║  echo "WARNING: Production environment!"                             ║
  ║  certbot --nginx -d ${var.domain}                                    ║
  ║  %{ else }                                                           ║
  ║  echo "Non-production deployment"                                    ║
  ║  %{ endif }                                                          ║
  ║  EOT                                                                 ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 3: Template for loop (%{ for ... in ... })                 ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  config = <<-EOT                                                      ║
  ║  %{ for mount in var.efs_mounts }                                    ║
  ║  mount -t efs ${mount.id}:/ ${mount.path}                            ║
  ║  %{ endfor }                                                         ║
  ║  EOT                                                                 ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 4: STRIP MARKER (~) — Remove whitespace before/after       ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  %{~ if condition ~}    ← Strip whitespace around the directive     ║
  ║  content                ← Only this line appears in output           ║
  ║  %{~ endif ~}           ← No extra blank lines in output             ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
🔤 Direct Interpolation — "${var.name}"

When you just need to embed a value into a string, "${...}" is the simplest approach. It evaluates ANY expression — not just variables. You can interpolate function calls, arithmetic, conditionals, and resource attributes. Terraform evaluates the expression, converts the result to a string, and inserts it inline.

"ami-${var.ami_id}" → "ami-0a1b2c3d"
"${var.env}-${var.region}" → "prod-us-east-1"
"v${var.major}.${var.minor}.${var.patch}" → "v1.7.0"
"${upper(var.env)}-v${var.version + 1}" → "PROD-v8"

💡 Tip: In modern Terraform (0.12+), you can omit the ${...} wrapper for top-level references: "ami-${var.id}" and "ami-var.id" — wait, that second one doesn't work. The ${...} is still required inside quoted strings. Outside strings, var.id alone is fine.

📄 Template Directives — %{ if } / %{ for }

When your generated string needs logic (conditionals, loops), template directives are the tool. They work inside heredoc strings (<<EOT ... EOT) and give you if/else/for control flow — turning a static template into a dynamic config generator. This is the standard way to generate EC2 user_data scripts, IAM policy documents, and Kubernetes manifests from Terraform.

# Available directives:
%{ if condition } ... %{ endif }
%{ if condition } ... %{ else } ... %{ endif }
%{ for item in list } ... %{ endfor }

💡 The ~ strip marker: %{~ if ... ~} removes whitespace before/after the directive — keeps output clean without extra blank lines. Always use %~ in production templates.

💡 Decision Rule: Interpolation vs Template vs templatefile()

Use "${var.x}" when embedding 1-3 values in a short string (tags, names, AMI IDs). Use %{ if } directives when you need conditional logic or loops in a multi-line string (user_data scripts). Use templatefile() when the template is large (>20 lines), complex, or shared across modules — it separates logic from config, making both cleaner. The exam may ask: "Which function renders a template file with variables?" — answer: templatefile().

10.2 Arithmetic & Logical Operators — Math and Boolean Logic

Terraform supports standard arithmetic and comparison operators. These are essential for computed values, conditional logic, and resource sizing calculations for anihpj/jobpost.

🔢 Arithmetic Operators
a + bAddition
a - bSubtraction
a * bMultiplication
a / bDivision (float result)
a % bModulus (remainder)
-aNegation
🔀 Comparison & Logical Operators
a == b / !=Equal / Not equal
a > b / <Greater / Less than
a >= b / <=Greater-or-equal / Less-or-equal
a && bLogical AND
a || bLogical OR
!aLogical NOT
anihpj/jobpost: Practical Operator Examples
# Compute K8s resource limits based on environment tier
locals {
  cpu_limit = var.environment == "prod" ? "1000m" : "500m"
  memory_multiplier = var.environment == "prod" ? 2 : 1
  total_memory = 256 * local.memory_multiplier  # 256 or 512 Mi

  # Multi-condition: backups needed for non-dev WITH flag enabled
  needs_backup = var.environment != "dev" && var.enable_backups
}

# Validation with logical operators
validation {
  condition     = var.replicas >= 1 && var.replicas <= 10
  error_message = "Replicas must be between 1 and 10 (inclusive)."
}

10.3 Conditional Expressions — Making Decisions in HCL

The conditional expression condition ? true_value : false_value is Terraform's if/else. It evaluates the condition as a boolean and returns one of two values. This is used everywhere: resource sizing, feature toggles, count decisions, and environment-specific configurations.

CONDITIONAL EXPRESSIONS — 5 Production-Ready Patterns
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  1. RESOURCE SIZING — Different sizes per environment               ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  instance_type = var.environment == "prod" ? "t3.medium" : "t3.micro"║
  ║  #              └───── condition ──────┘  └── true ──┘  └── false ──┘║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  2. CONDITIONAL RESOURCE CREATION — count = 1 or 0                  ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  resource "aws_cloudwatch_dashboard" "anihpj" {                      ║
  ║    count = var.environment == "prod" ? 1 : 0                         ║
  ║    dashboard_name = "anihpj-${terraform.workspace}"                  ║
  ║  }                                                                   ║
  ║  # count=0 means: do NOT create this resource at all                ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  3. FEATURE TOGGLE — Enable/disable features                        ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  backup_retention_period = var.enable_backups ? 30 : 0               ║
  ║  deletion_protection     = var.environment == "prod" ? true : false  ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  4. DEFAULT VALUE WITH FALLBACK                                     ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  ami = var.custom_ami != "" ? var.custom_ami : data.aws_ami.latest.id║
  ║  #    └── condition ──┘    └── true ──┘   └── false/default ──┘     ║
  ║  💡 A cleaner alternative: coalesce(var.custom_ami, data.aws_ami...) ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  5. NESTED CONDITIONALS — Multi-way branching                        ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  instance_type = (                                                   ║
  ║    var.environment == "prod"    ? "t3.large"  :                      ║
  ║    var.environment == "staging" ? "t3.medium" :                      ║
  ║    "t3.micro"                     # default (dev)                    ║
  ║  )                                                                   ║
  ║  ⚠️  Better approach: use lookup() with a map for 3+ branches!      ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

10.4 For Expressions — Transforming Lists & Maps

for expressions iterate over collections and produce new collections. They're the functional programming backbone of HCL — used for filtering, mapping, grouping, and transforming data in a single expression.

FOR EXPRESSIONS — The Complete Reference Card
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 1: LIST → LIST (transform with :)                          ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  [for env in ["dev", "staging", "prod"] : upper(env)]               ║
  ║  → ["DEV", "STAGING", "PROD"]                                       ║
  ║  Syntax: [ for  in  :  ]                   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 2: LIST → LIST (filter with if)                             ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  [for cidr in var.subnets : cidr if length(cidr) > 0]              ║
  ║  Syntax: [ for  in  :  if  ]         ║
  ║  # Only items satisfying the condition are included                  ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  PATTERN 3: MAP → MAP (transform with =>)                            ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  {for env, size in var.instance_types : env => upper(size)}         ║
  ║  Input:  {dev = "t3.micro", prod = "t3.medium"}                     ║
  ║  Output: {dev = "T3.MICRO", prod = "T3.MEDIUM"}                     ║
  ║  Syntax: { for , in  :  =>  }   ║
  ║  💡 {} outputs a MAP; [] outputs a LIST                              ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
🧭 When to Use Which For Expression Pattern
You want to...Use this pattern
Transform every item in a list[for x in list : transform(x)]
Filter a list (keep some, drop others)[for x in list : x if condition]
Convert list → map (keyed by attribute){for x in list : x.key => x}
Transform map values, keep same keys{for k,v in map : k => transform(v)}
Group items by a common property{for x in list : x.group => x...}
⚠️ Common For Expression Mistakes

1. Wrong bracket type: [for...] creates a LIST, {for...} creates a MAP. Using [] when you need {} produces a type error downstream.

2. Missing => in map for: {for x in list : x.key x.value} — the => arrow between key and value is required syntax.

3. Filter before transform: If you filter AND transform, the if clause comes AFTER the result expression: [for x in list : upper(x) if x != ""].

4. Null elements crash: If any element in the source list is null and you access x.attribute, the for expression errors. Wrap with try() or filter with if x != null.

5. Use locals for readability: Nested for expressions are hard to read. Break them into named locals — your teammates will thank you.

anihpj/jobpost: Real-World For Expressions
# Get all private IPs of running EC2 instances
output "private_ips" {
  value = [for instance in aws_instance.anihpj : instance.private_ip]
}

# Create namespace → pod-count map from K8s namespace labels
locals {
  ns_pod_map = {
    for ns in kubernetes_namespace.anihpj :
    ns.metadata[0].name => ns.metadata[0].labels["pod-count"]
  }
}

# Filter to only production subnets
locals {
  prod_subnets = [
    for subnet in data.aws_subnets.all.ids :
    subnet if can(regex("prod", subnet))
  ]
}

10.5 Splat Expressions [*] — Extracting Attributes from Resource Lists

The splat expression [*] is a shorthand for extracting a single attribute from every element of a list or map. It's equivalent to a for expression but more concise.

SPLAT [*] vs FOR — Two Ways to Extract Attributes
  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  THE SPLAT WAY (shorter, preferred for simple extraction):           ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  aws_instance.web[*].id          → ["i-abc", "i-def", "i-ghi"]     ║
  ║  aws_instance.web[*].public_ip   → ["54.1.2.3", "54.4.5.6"]        ║
  ║                                                                      ║
  ║  # Works on both:                                                    ║
  ║  # count-based resources: aws_instance.web[*].id                     ║
  ║  # for_each-based resources: aws_instance.web[*].id (same syntax!)  ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
  ║  THE FOR WAY (longer, for complex transformations):                  ║
  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  [for inst in aws_instance.web : inst.id]    ← Same as splat [*]   ║
  ║  [for inst in aws_instance.web : "${inst.id}:${inst.public_ip}"]   ║
  ║  # For expressions are better when you need to combine attributes   ║
  ╚══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗

10.6 Built-in Functions — The Terraform Function Library

Terraform ships with 100+ built-in functions organized into categories. You don't import them — they're available globally in any expression. The exam tests your knowledge of the most commonly used ones.

anihpj/jobpost: Functions in Action
# Generate S3 bucket name (must be globally unique)
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "assets" {
  bucket = "anihpj-${var.environment}-assets-${random_id.suffix.hex}"
  # Uses: join() implicitly, random_id resource
}

# CIDR math for subnet allocation
locals {
  vpc_cidr = "10.0.0.0/16"
  public_subnets  = [for i in range(3) : cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 8, i)]
  private_subnets = [for i in range(3) : cidrsubnet(local.vpc_cidr, 8, i + 3)]
  # → ["10.0.0.0/24", "10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24"]  (public)
  # → ["10.0.3.0/24", "10.0.4.0/24", "10.0.5.0/24"]  (private)
}

# Template rendering for user_data
user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/user_data.sh.tftpl", {
  environment = var.environment
  db_host     = aws_db_instance.anihpj.address
  docker_tag  = var.jobpost_config.docker.image_tag
})
TEMPLATEFILE() — Dynamic Configuration Generation (Exam Favorite!)

  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  #!/bin/bash                                                       ║
  ║  echo "Deploying ${app_name} in ${environment}"                    ║
  ║  echo "Database host: ${db_host}"                                   ║
  ║  echo "Redis host: ${redis_host}"                                   ║

  ╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗

  ╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
  ║  user_data = templatefile("${path.module}/user_data.sh.tftpl", {    ║
  ║    app_name    = "anihpj"                                           ║
  ║    environment = var.environment                                    ║
  ║    db_host     = aws_db_instance.pg.address                         ║
  ║    redis_host  = aws_elasticache_cluster.redis.address              ║

  ║  ✅ Real DB/Redis endpoints injected                                ║
  ║  ✅ SSL config ONLY for prod (conditional %{ if })                  ║
  ║  ✅ EFS mounts generated from list (loop %{ for })                  ║
  ║  ✅ Separation of logic (template) from values (.tf file)           ║
